subsubtopic: COMMUNITY ANTENNA TELEVISION-DISPUTE WITH QUEBEC RESPECTING JURISDICTION-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you will recall that on February 23 last I tabled a copy of a letter I had sent to the Hon. Jean-Paul L'Allier, the Quebec Minister of Communications, informing him that the government had taken note of an ordinance issued to community-antenna-television operators by the Public Service Board of Quebec which constitutes a clear attempt to super-impose provincial jurisdiction on an area of exclusive federal legislative authority.
The Public Service Board of Quebec has now issued to most of the community-antenna-television operators in the province a form of temporary certificate purporting to authorize them to continue operating pending the issuance of a permanent provincial licence, for which application will have to be made before a date not yet determined.
Federal legislative authority over radio communications and broadcasting, including community-antenna-television undertakings, has been upheld in all the relevant decisions of the courts. In our view, these actions by the Public Service Board of Quebec, with the support of the responsible Quebec minister, are consequently ultra vires and represent an encroachment on federal authority which the government intends to resist by all the means at
its disposal. In practical terms, the issuance of an operating certificate or licence by the Public Service Board of Quebec, or its failure or refusal to issue such a certificate or licence, is irrelevant in so far as the Canadian RadioTelevision Commission is concerned in exercising its authority.

It is particularly disappointing that this unilateral action should have been taken by a single province at a time when the government has put forward its proposals for means of collaborating with the provinces on communications policies and regulatory procedures which will give due effect to legitimate provincial interests. These proposals have been generally welcomed by the governments of the provinces, which are now engaged in preparation for substantive federal-provincial discussions in the fall.
In these circumstances, the government is not prepared to accept unilateral action by any province. The government is, nevertheless, quite willing to enter into discussion with the government of Quebec with a view to determining the most appropriate means for having the constitutional issue involved in this matter settled by the courts, the governments of the other provinces being kept informed of these discussions.
I further wish to give notice that in the event the government of Quebec persists in its intended action, the government will not hesitate to initiate appropriate action on its own behalf including action in the courts, if necessary.

subsubtopic: COMMUNITY ANTENNA TELEVISION-DISPUTE WITH QUEBEC RESPECTING JURISDICTION-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the minister on behalf of our party for making a copy of his statement available to us in advance of its delivery. In the normal course, the response from our party would be made by the hon. member for Annapolis Valley who is unavoidably absent.
My colleagues and I share the minister's concern over the unilateral decision of the province of Quebec with regard to licencing of community antenna stations. But we must express as well our very deep concern that there appears to exist a serious breakdown here that could affect the development of broadcasting policy throughout Canada for some time. We are particularly concerned that this should have occurred so soon after the tabling in the House of the government's green paper on communication policy. We can only conclude that the action of the government of Quebec is a reaction to the green paper, or that the green paper was developed in isolation and that in many respects the policy position established is one that is not based on any coherent understanding of the position of the provincial government on the matter.


Community Antenna Television Conflict
This whole matter raises very serious questions about the future of an integrated broadcasting policy in the country and it raises questions that the minister has not addressed in his statement as to the reaction of the other provinces. I think that one thing is clear: we cannot have chaos in our communication policy in Canada. It will be necessary to work out a policy that can be agreed to by all provinces and the federal government. I think it is a matter to note in the House that the federal government has had five years to work out an agreement on this matter, and obviously on the evidence today it has failed to do so.
It is clear that members of the House and the people of Canada have the right to much more information on this matter. We certainly request the minister to keep us advised of and in close touch with the developments in negotiations with the province of Quebec and with any other province concerned. I would also express the hope that, should the Standing Committee on Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts make the request, the minister himself will be prepared to go into the matter in some detail before the members of that committee.

subsubtopic: COMMUNITY ANTENNA TELEVISION-DISPUTE WITH QUEBEC RESPECTING JURISDICTION-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we regret that there is this dispute between the government of Canada and the government of Quebec, but I must say that in our view the position stated in the minister's remarks this morning is a correct one so far as the constitutional position is concerned. Indeed, it is in line with the relevant decisions of the courts. However, we are glad to know that the government is making arrangements for discussions with the governments of all the provinces with respect to this matter and, in particular, that even though this dispute has reached a rather warm point the government is prepared to enter into discussions with the government of Quebec in the hope that the matter can be resolved without having to take it to the courts. We wish the government of Canada and the government of Quebec well in their efforts to resolve this dispute.

subsubtopic: COMMUNITY ANTENNA TELEVISION-DISPUTE WITH QUEBEC RESPECTING JURISDICTION-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for our part, we are somewhat surprised with the statement of the Minister of Communications (Mr. Pelletier) on the problem that exists with regard to Quebec. That statement, in a few words, means that the federal government says no to what Quebec has asked with regard to a cable TV service.
Contrary to the hon. members who spoke before us, we are far from sure that the federal government is right when Quebec is only asking one thing, the jurisdiction that is properly its own, that is, education.
As for the news release of this morning, and particularly its last paragraph, unfortunately I cannot say I agree with it. Indeed, it says, and I quote:
-the government will not hesitate to initiate appropriate action on its own behalf including action in the courts, if necessary.
Mr. Speaker, according to me the end of this statement is extremely overbearing. The federal government wants to deal with a problem over which it is not yet sure to have jurisdiction, namely that of community antennas and education, which is the responsibility of provincial governments. If one is to speak about co-operative federalism, I

do not think threats bordering on blackmail should be delivered.
The federal government declares that it will not hesitate to initiate proper action, including legal action if need be, to justify its position. In my opinion, this is a very arrogant attitude that endangers beforehand those agreements which could be reached by other more normal means.
We regret very much the last section of that statement, and if under other circumstances the same methods were applied and the same arrogance shown towards other provinces, I am sure that there would be an outcry across Canada in order to settle federal provincial relations, for I think the statement made this morning will seriously affect future federal provincial relations.
It is most unfortunate that in such an area as broadcasting which in the first place was of provincial jurisdiction, the federal government has assumed those responsibilities because the provinces did not exercise theirs over that matter at the right time. Today the federal government takes over a jurisdiction which was a provincial one in the first place.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that we may see from this statement new evidence that the federal government infringes upon the provincial jurisdiction, and that it is a centralizing government at a time when it advocates decentralization.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Marshall (Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe) moved:
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO IMPROVE PENSIONS AND REMOVE INJUSTICES TO WAR VETERANS
speechtext:
That this House urges the government to introduce priority measures to remedy present injustices to war veterans and, in particular, to remove those inequities arising out of basic rates of disability and other pensions, treatment services, allowances, and the Veterans' Land Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, my party's motion today is introduced as an appeal to the government in an attempt to emphasize the need to fulfil a commitment made over 50 years ago to a special citizen of our country, the war veteran, a citizen who sadly is becoming less and less recognized at a time when he needs recognition most in his declining years. The motion reads:
That this House urges the government to introduce priority measures to remedy present injustices to war veterans and, in particular, to remove those inequities arising out of basic rates of disability and other pensions, treatment services, allowances, and the Veterans' Land Act.
I am sure everyone will agree that Veterans Affairs is one legislative area that has been non-controversial. In dealing with such legislation over the years, there certainly has been an atmosphere of co-operation regardless of party lines. I believe that, as a group of former soldiers learned in the use of military strategy, we veterans have been wrong in our attempt to have the government of the


War Veterans
day fulfill a commitment to war veterans made over 50 years ago, a commitment that Canada owed as a matter of right. The government deserves all possible support in their efforts to rehabilitate veterans in return for their fulfillment of their patriotic duty to our great country. The fulfillment of this commitment would allow them not only a decent living but an equal opportunity to re-enter society and to live a rich, full life along with other Canadians whose best years were not disturbed during the war.
So what have we done? For over 50 years we have followed the "nibble philosophy" because the original drafters of the veterans charter could not see far enough ahead, through no fault of their own, to design a plan which would deal with future needs of veterans in a changing society. However, no one is blaming these legislators, and over the years many good things have come about. Those who came before us and represented veterans in the House of Commons have served the veterans well and are held in the highest esteem.
Without casting blame on anyone, we must be big enough to admit that we have failed in many areas and now it is almost too late to make amends. However, we can correct the many inequities which exist at present. We have a chance to clear them up once and for all by showing a little human consideration and by stopping to think once in a while of the veteran for whom it is our duty to care.
Recently, we passed a bill to increase war veterans allowances, and we passed it in record time. Members from all parties gave complete support to the amendments to the act. We even threw bouquets across the floor to the minister and his government for bringing in the following amendments. First, we proposed that the bill increase benefits under the act to a maximum allowable of $2,293.68 for the single veteran and $3,926.52 for the married veteran. In addition, the table of allowances gave annual increments to orphans of veterans on an annual basis. Second, we proposed that the amendments allow exemptions to veterans on reaching the age of 65 of $15 if single and $30 if married. Third, we proposed that casual earnings be increased to allow the veteran or his wife to earn increased amounts up to $1,000 for the single veteran and $1,500 for the married veteran.
However, there are still a few inequities in the War Veteran Allowances Act which need revision, and by offering the first point of my party's motion we urge the government to introduce priority measures to remedy the following. First, the removal of the Canadian residence requirement for war veterans living abroad, which would involve the amendment of section 3(1) of the War Veterans Allowances Act. It is possible for a veteran to qualify for an allowance by returning to Canada for one year, and subsequently the benefit is continued even though the recipient may take up permanent residence outside the country. Although the required year's residence may be met without difficulty in border areas, it is more difficult for veterans long distances away to meet these requirements. Benefits first became payable outside of Canada through an amendment back in 1960 to permit the continuation of payment of allowances outside Canada primarily for reasons of health or family ties. As of January 1973 there were only 709 persons receiving allowances

outside Canada. An amendment to the legislation removing the 12 month residence will extend the benefit to Canadian veterans who are unable to return to Canada to qualify.
Second, an amendment must be brought forth which would enable a surviving spouse to receive an allowance for a surviving child who is attending an educational institution, even though that child is 21 years of age. We must increase that age limit to 25 years or to the time when the child ceases to attend an educational institution. Surely, the government could provide these benefits until the age of 25, as is presently the case under the war dead educational assistance act, particularly when the number involved are so small. Surely, we must realize the basic need to extend this age limit to 25 without the need for any dramatic explanation or elaboration.
Third, the requirement for 365 service days should be eliminated and service in the United Kingdom before November 12, 1918, should be accepted as a qualification for world war I veterans.
The average age of world war I recipients of veterans allowance is 78.4 years, and it is unlikely that it would be much lower in the case of those with limited service in the United Kingdom. The removal of the one year clause would not apply to many veterans, and since almost all of them would be receiving OAS benefits, the cost involved would be small. However, it would provide a certain degree of additional comfort to these elderly recipients, and it would provide them with drugs and other assistance to which they are entitled now.
If these three inequities were corrected, we would have a good act fulfilling our commitment to these veterans once and for all. Surely, our consciences should dictate that we make these amendments in the next few months.
The greatest failure that exists in the present legislation has to do with the basic rate of pensions, and this was one of the main reasons for our motion today. The throne speech committed the government to increases in disability pensions as well as war veterans allowances, but here we are four months later having made no progress in this respect. I can only say that the government has callously reneged on its responsibility.
We have before us today a joint study report on the basic rate of pensions. It was conducted on the authority of the previous minister of veterans affairs and with the accord of the present minister, the chairman of the pension committee, a representative of veterans organizations and others. These individuals and groups brought before the standing committee recommendations that were reasonable and that, most important, were unanimously accepted by everyone concerned.
The report was signed by eight responsible and dedicated Canadians, including the representatives of the Department of Veterans Affairs, the Canadian Pension Commission and of all veterans organizations. They submitted a report which, in the main recommended the following points. First, the basic rate of pension should be established, on the basis of an average of a composite group of public servants, for the single pensioner at $4,529 a year. This is an increase over the present rate of $3,793. Second, the married rate of pension should be established at the


single rate plus 25 per cent. Third, the additional pension for children should be established at 13 per cent for one child, 22.5 per cent for two children, and for each additional child an additional 7.5 per cent. Rates should also be established for the widow of the veteran, the dependant parent, and dependant children. Furthermore, a recommendation was included in the report that pensions should be adjusted annually on a fixed date in accordance with changes in the average wage rates for the selected public service group, rather than on the basis of adjustments in the cost of living.
These recommendations were made after three months of study by a responsible group and referred to the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs. They were accepted unanimously by all parties. Remember, Mr. Speaker, that the deputy minister of the Department of Veterans Affairs, the chairman of the Pension Commission, who was also chairman of the group, and the representative of all veterans organizations gave their signatures of approval. Remember also, Mr. Speaker, that the recommendations were referred to the Standing Committee and, without debate, accepted in record time after only token comments supporting the report by government and opposition parties. The Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) himself attended the meetings of the committee and supported the recommendations without question.
However, where do we stand today? We find ourselves in a dilemma. The legislation promised in the throne speech has not yet been produced. Why is that? Because the Liberal party hierarchy, the cabinet, will not accept the recommendation which proposes the new formula based on annual increases in accordance with the average wage rather than on the increases in the cost of living. This is the dilemma. They will not support the recommendations of the minister, of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs representing all parties, of the Chairman of the Pension Commission who is charged with the responsibility of dealing with the applications of thousands of veterans who submit claims, nor of the veterans' organizations of Canada, representing over 900,000 veterans.
Reports from the inner circle indicate that the strongest opponent to these recommendations is the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury), a former top ranking officer in the Canadian army who led thousands of veterans during the Second World War. He, of all people, is opposing the justified increases to his comrades who followed him during that war, and if I were not a responsible member of parliament I would say something I know I should not say.
My party's motion therefore is justified in requesting priority measures to remedy this injustice. I plead with the minister, with the house leader and with the President of the Treasury Board that, if any legislation is ready for introduction to this House, it had better include all the recommendations of the joint study report or it will not be acceptable. Further, if after indicating, as the government did, that it will produce legislation before the summer recess, and this legislation does not include those recommendations, then I say to members of the government that
War Veterans
they will not be fulfilling their commitment to the veterans of Canada.
Moving to another important phase of responsibility relating to disability pensions, it is the responsibility of the Pension Commission and of the Pensions Review Board to deal with new applications for pensions arising out of the Woods Committee report and recommendations. While we have been willing to accept the reasons given for delays, it is now time to take the necessary action to deal with these recommendations on a higher priority than presently exists. In spite of corrective action being taken by the addition of members to the Pension Commission, and in spite of the determined efforts of the Commission, the government must extend every effort to increase the capability of the Commission because too many veterans are dying while awaiting for its decisions. This, again, is a priority measure which must be introduced to remedy present injustices to veterans, as well as the injustices caused by the delays in respect of the treatment of prisoners of war. It is a shame that only now, at this late date, is a study being conducted into the condition of former European prisoners of war.
Another serious inequity has to do with the Veterans Land Act. The present legislation is completely out-dated, and rather than providing the relief necessary in the present period of inflation, veterans are stultified in their efforts to build a home because of the failure of the government to provide for rising costs in the act. Part II of the act provides that any qualified veteran who is approved for a loan under the National Housing Act may receive financial and other assistance to build his own home, on any lot acceptable for a single family dwelling. The amount that may be advanced is $18,000 or the amount of the NHA loan, whichever is the lesser.
The act provides also that a veteran must acquire a lot of one half acre, but in certain cases this can be reduced by 20 per cent. My question to the minister is this: how can anyone build a home for $18,000 at present costs, or how can any veteran acquire a lot of one half acre, less 20 per cent, at present costs before he even starts to build a home? This also brings into focus the terminal date for initial applications for assistance which is set at March 31, 1974. There are some 125,000 veterans with qualification certificates and, according to the annual report of the department, it is expected that only 5 per cent will take advantage of the VLA.
The reason for this is that the loan ceiling is too low in view of present day inflation. Further, the size of building lots required is unrealistic, and the down payment is entirely too high. The government must immediately review the act with a view to (1) raising the ceiling to an acceptable level which, in view of today's inflationary costs, might be $25,000 or $30,000; (2) reducing the size of the lot to that of a normal building lot; (3) changing the down payments to at least today's level, and in line with the National Housing Act; (4) extending the termination date of March, 1974 to a period commensurate with the needs of present Canadian Forces personnel when retiring; and (5) giving consideration to inserting a rehabilitation program into the act to allow veterans to repair their present homes, in the case of need, along the lines stipulated in the National Housing Act. speakeroldname: Hon. Daniel J. MacDonald (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO IMPROVE PENSIONS AND REMOVE INJUSTICES TO WAR VETERANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, some hon. members appear to be under the impression that the Veterans Charter is a monolithic affair that has been left virtually unchanged for a generation or more and is now hopelessly out of date. Nothing could be farther from the truth.
The government has been keeping the Veterans Charter under continuous review, and a great number of changes have been made from year to year as the need has presented itself. I might add also that the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs has played a very active part in making sure at all times that veterans' problems are fully aired and sympathetically considered, and I am glad to express the government's thanks to the committee for its helpful contributions.
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, the Veterans Affairs budget had been rising from year to year, and I would expect that it would continue to do so for some years to come. The departmental expenditure budget has risen almost continuously from $396 million in 1966-67 to $480 million in the current year. Over the years there has been a slight reduction in total staff because of hospital transfers, but the authorized total still stands at 10,455 man years. I propose at this time to review some of the more important changes that have been made in the Veterans Charter during the past few years. First, I will deal with the area of disability pensions.
Since 1944, hardly a single year has passed without new legislation to up-date some aspect of the Pension Act. Then, between 1968 and 1970, the entire act was reviewed in great detail by the Woods Committee which presented no less than 146 proposed changes. The ensuing legislation, which received Royal Assent on March 30, 1971, just two years ago, represented the consummation of the most thorough review of the pension legislation in 50 years.
These main amendments had many far reaching effects, but I should at least mention the introduction of the exceptional incapacity allowance, the broadening of the

benefit of the doubt rule, the special arrangements made for Hong Kong prisoners of war, the establishment of the independent Bureau of Pension Advocates and the Pension Review Board. Just last year, as one of the measures, parliament enacted legislation to provide for the first time that the rates of pension would be adjusted in January of every year to reflect upward changes in the consumer price index. Pursuant to this legislation, pension rates were raised by 3.6 per cent last year, and again by 4.5 per cent in January of this year. There will be another adjustment next January, and in every future year. This legislation ties disability pensions to the cost of living, so that they retain their real value from year to year. I need hardly add that the whole matter of the basic rate of pensions is at present under very active consideration by the government. I have already informed the House that I hope in the very near future to be in a position to make an announcement on this subject.
So much for pensions. Let me turn next to War Veterans Allowance, the so-called "burnt-out pension". There have been no less than four increases in WVA rates in the last two years. As in the case of pensions, the WVA Act was amended last year to provide that rates would be escalated each year as indicated by rises in the cost of living, and they were accordingly increased by 3.6 per cent last year and by a further 4.5 per cent in January, 1973. Just a month and a half ago a further large increase took effect, as was mentioned by the hon. member who spoke previously, in the same amounts as the increases under the Old Age Security Act. At the same time the act was amended to remove the "personal property" qualification, so that applicants would no longer be required to liquidate their assets before becoming eligible for War Veterans Allowance. In other words, the long standing "needs test" has been replaced by a modified "income test". We have also been conducting a large advertising campaign in veterans publications, in weekend supplements, in the farm press and on the radio, to make certain that veterans were fully informed on these changes.
With reference to our hospital transfer negotiations, I should like to take this opportunity to clear up a misunderstanding. Our purpose in seeking to transfer veterans' hospitals to local and regional authorities is not to get rid of the hospitals or to reduce our responsibility. Quite the contrary, our aim is to ensure that veterans continue to receive the best possible hospital care. If these institutions were to continue indefinitely as veterans hospitals, the average age of the patients would rise continuously and the hospitals would become geriatric institutions. On this basis, we would gradually lose our ability to attract and retain the best doctors, nurses and paramedical staff, and then the quality of the care of veterans would inevitably suffer. The only alternative is to blend the hospitals into the communities in which they stand, so that they may continue as active treatment hospitals for both veterans and others. Of course, in any transfer agreement the government ensures that a sufficient number of priority -beds remain available to meet the needs of the veterans, and the government insists that the present hospital staff is taken over by the new authority without reduction in salary. I need hardly add that, following transfer, the


government continues to pay the treatment costs of entitled veterans.
Now, I should like to say a word about the Veterans Land Act. In recent weeks I have received a certain number of letters urging that the statute be amended to continue this program beyond the terminal dates specified in the legislation.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO IMPROVE PENSIONS AND REMOVE INJUSTICES TO WAR VETERANS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO IMPROVE PENSIONS AND REMOVE INJUSTICES TO WAR VETERANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe that these requests, understandable though they are, have been based on misapprehensions regarding the aims of this program. The act was not designed as a program of urban housing, nor as a part of a retirement program for persons reaching the end of their productive careers. It was designed to provide financial assistance for the purchase of agricultural land to be used on a full time or part time farming basis by veterans. The purpose was to help them pick up the threads of civilian life following active service. Realizing that not all veterans would wish to use the Veterans Land Act, parliament enacted two other measures, re-establishment credits and postwar university training. I might note here, Mr. Speaker, that most of the letters I received from people wanting to construct under the Veterans Land Act illustrate three things that were available to all veterans. One was to establish them in part time or full time farming; another was to rehabilitate them through university training, and another one was money. In many many cases, we found upon investigation that one or other of these benefits had been received by practically all the veterans who wrote to me. A veteran could use only one of the three measures.
Recognizing that the act was intended as a measure of rehabilitation assistance in the period after wartime active service, as distinct from retirement from postwar occupations or careers, in 1965, eight years ago, parliament established the March 31, 1974 deadline for the purpose of phasing out Veterans Land Act lending operations in an orderly manner. By that date, almost 30 years will have elapsed since the end of the World War II, and 20 years in the case of the Korean conflict.
In the time at my disposal, I cannot of course cover all aspects of departmental operations. I should like, however, to say something about remembrance. First, let me say that each year during the past ten years the government has conducted ceremonies to commemorate the deeds and sacrifices of Canada's veterans, and in each year these ceremonies have been held in Canada and in the places where they fell. Last year my predecessor attended ceremonies in France to commemorate the landings at Dieppe. Within a few weeks I am taking a small delegation to Normandy, where as guests of the government of France we shall be marking the anniversary of the D-Day landings. Later this year, I hope to inspect a number of the cemeteries and memorials in Europe that are maintained at Canadian expense to commemorate the contributions by the thousands of Canadians ip two world conflicts.
Mr. Speaker, I have said that the government keeps the Veterans Charter under constant review, and I believe what I have said will amply confirm the point. I can also assure the House that we shall continue to keep all these measures under review. The government fully recognizes
War Veterans
its responsibility to its veterans and to their loved ones. We have been fulfilling that responsibility and will continue to do so.
Now, Mr. Speaker, to refer to some of the points brought out by the hon. member who moved the motion. With regard to the overseas veterans, as I have said in the Veterans Affairs Committee, this has been and is presently under review. As far as additional money for the children to age 25, that is in the same situation.
I want to make reference to the Pension Commission, also referred to by the hon. gentleman who proposed the resolution. We realize that there is a lot of concern on the part of veterans, veterans associations and people across the country that applications are not being processed as rapidly as many of us would desire. However, the House knows that we have added quite a number of people to the Pension Commission and it takes time to train them to deal with this situation and to understand the legislation. We have appointed people who are capable of assessing medical information and bringing the cases concerned to the attention of individuals looking after the pension matter. We are doing our utmost here. According to the last report I have had, pension applications are now being approved a little faster than we are receiving them. Many of those veterans, I have to say with respect, are and have been in receipt of pensions, possibly for a quarter of a century or more. It sounds bad to hear that so many are behind. At the same time, that does not mean that the veterans are starving. In many cases, we have a priority list. We bring urgent pension cases to the top of the list when they are brought to our attention.
It seems to us, in the department, that we have begun to cope with this situation in a much better way than in the past, and we are certainly going to get on top of it. I can say that the Pension Commission is very conscious of this, as is the pension chairman. I have the highest regard for him and know he is dedicated. Many members on the other side of the House, as well as on my side, know that many of these files are extremely thick. Sometimes, when there is no medical evidence to support an application, you have to look for people all over the country who served with the applicant. That is a very difficult job.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to commend the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall) for the motion he has presented to the House today. I also commend him on the speech he made on introducing his motion. Those of us in all parties in this House who are concerned about the welfare of our veterans welcome the opportunity presented to us today to discuss a number of matters that are of deep concern. Those last few words indicate that there are quite a number of issues relating to veterans that will be discussed. However, I agree with the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe that the

War Veterans
main purpose in bringing forward this motion today, the main thrust of the speeches that will be made, I trust, by members on both sides of the House, is that we want no more delay on the part of the government in bringing forward the bill to amend the Pension Act, the purpose of which is to increase the basic amount of the war disability pension.
The hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe pointed out, as all hon. members are aware, that this legislation has been promised since the day the present session began. Early in January, the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) indicated that the report of the special joint study group on the basic rate of the war disability pension would be referred to the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs. That was done within a few days of the making of that promise. That committee took only an hour or two to make its report back to the House, unanimously supporting the recommendation in that report. The minister was present at the meeting and it was clear that he shared the view of all on the committee that it was an excellent report and should be implemented at the earliest possible date.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), when making his budget speech on February 19, indicated that the government was only waiting for the report from the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs before acting. That report came down just a few days after the budget speech.
When we asked the Minister of Veterans Affairs questions prior to the Easter recess about the introduction of the bill to raise the basic rate of the war disability pension, he expressed the hope that he would be able to do it before Easter. Well, Easter is a movable feast, but it did not move quite that far. It has come and gone, and we are still without the legislation. Yesterday, in response to yet another question of mine, the minister said that he hoped to bring the bill in, if I may use his exact words, "before very long". When I asked him whether "before very long" means this month, he replied:
Mr. Speaker, I would indicate that I am hopeful that it certainly means this month.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO IMPROVE PENSIONS AND REMOVE INJUSTICES TO WAR VETERANS
speechtext: The House leader said it would be brought in before the recess.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO IMPROVE PENSIONS AND REMOVE INJUSTICES TO WAR VETERANS
speechtext:
Here we are, on May 18; the minister has 13 days left in which to do this. I am glad to see the President of the Treasury (Mr. Drury) sitting here and listening to the debate, because he will realize how keen the House is to have this piece of legislation introduced.
As has already been pointed out, the recommendation of the joint study group, which was supported by the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs, calls for the basic rate of the war disability pension to be tied to the average rate of pay of five selected categories in the public service. That, indeed, is an attempt to fulfil a promise that has been around more than 50 years. I certainly join with all those who, over the years, have spoken on this matter, but I now say that we hope there will not be another arbitrary figure picked by the government and put in the legislation. This time we want what the joint study group has recommended, namely, that the basic rate of the war

disability pension be tied to the average annual income of five selected categories in the public service.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO IMPROVE PENSIONS AND REMOVE INJUSTICES TO WAR VETERANS
speechtext: They are not those of deputy ministers, either.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO IMPROVE PENSIONS AND REMOVE INJUSTICES TO WAR VETERANS
speechtext:
No. I trust that remark is on the record. We are talking about five groups down near the bottom of the ladder.
The report pointed out that war disability pensions are not subject to income tax and that, therefore, in arriving at a figure a certain adjustment has to be made in what would be the gross average pay of those working in those five groups. For 1972, this worked out to the figure of $4,529 per year. There have been pay adjustments since then, so that for 1973 the figure would be a little higher. The amount of $4,529 represents an increase of 19.4 per cent over the amount now being paid as the 100 per cent basic rate. I would hope that, considering the increases which have taken place in wage rates this year, the figure might be somewhat higher still.
The important thing about this recommendation is not just the suggested figure, which is roughly 20 per cent higher than that in the present legislation. The important thing about it is that it recommends that that basic rate be tied to those rates of pay I have mentioned, so that in future years the basic rate will go up, as those rates of pay go up. This is well covered on pages 20 and 21 of the report of the joint study group which was signed by the nine persons to whom my hon. friend referred a few moments ago. May I point out, as well, that it is no longer good enough just to give veterans an increase equal only to the rise in the cost of living. Rather, they should be given increases that are related to the rising standard of living. The joint study group points out that the best way to do that is to tie the basic rate of the war disability pension to the average of the rates mentioned in the public service.
I liked the approach of the minister this morning in making it clear to us that the government has not forgotten these things. I liked his confirmation of his statement to me of yesterday that the bill is to be brought in soon. Yesterday he said that that "means this month", the month of May. I must say to him, however, that I am concerned, indeed, disturbed, that he stands up this late in the game and boasts about the clause in the Pension Act that provides for the basic rate to be escalated according to the rise in the cost of living. He should not still be boasting about that. The report of the joint study group, which included the Deputy Minister of Veterans Affairs, as well as Mr. Solomon, and three or four others, said that that is not good enough. I suspect that is the reason for the delay. I suspect this bothers the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury). He does not mind giving an increase, but he is worried about this formula that would provide automatic increases in future years in accordance with the rise in the rates of pay of these selected groups. That is the whole issue. It is not just an issue because this study group recommended it. It has been an issue for more than half a century that the basic disability pension should be tied to certain levels of income and not just be a figure that the government can hand out from time to time by amending the act. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I strongly urge


the minister to insist that his bill implement in full the recommendation of the joint study group.
I hope that as a result of today's debate, which is being listened to by the Minister of Veterans Affairs and the President of the Treasury Board, the bill will be brought in soon and that it will have in it the formula recommended in the report of the joint study group. The hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe said that if this is not done, the bill will not be acceptable. We will find that out if we have to go through the sorry situation of the bill not being satisfactory when it goes to committee and the veterans organizations appear before that committee. My suspicion is that if the bill just contains an arbitrary figure without accepting the recommended formula, the veterans organizations will appear before us with some pretty strong representations. All of that can be avoided and the 50 year promise can be kept, if the government will bring in the bill recommended by the joint study group and strongly endorsed by the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs. That is the main purpose of the motion before us today. I hope it will be the main purpose and main thrust of the debate.
All of us who will take the floor today are concerned about a number of other matters, and we shall have a few words to say about some of those matters. In particular, my colleague, the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters), will have a good deal to say about the Veterans Land Act and what needs to be done with regard to it. There are a few other matters on which I think a comment or two should be made.
With regard to the War Veterans Allowance Act, we welcomed at the time and we are still glad that increases were made in the basic rate of the war veterans allowance. But like other members, I am receiving letters from veterans who are wondering why they did not get the increase. They thought there was an increase. Those over 65 years of age are glad that the ceiling was raised. This permits them to get the full amount of the old age security and guaranteed supplement increase. However, there is no increase for them in their war veterans allowances. The minister covered that very nicely in the letter he sent to veterans with their April cheques. He referred to the changes that had been made and then wrote this interesting sentence:
At the same time, Old Age Security and Guaranteed Income Supplement combined payments were increased by the same amounts; which means that those of you who are aged 65 and over will find their increases in those cheques, instead of in their WVA/CWA payments,-
The rest of the sentence states that those payments would not be decreased. That is a nice euphemistic public service way of saying you will not be getting an increase in your war veterans allowance. It is true that those under 65 who are not at the ceiling will get an adjustment because of the higher rates. However, I feel it would have been appropriate to raise the ceiling on the permissible income under the War Veterans Allowance Act, not just by the amount of the increase in the old age security and guaranteed supplement adjustment, but by an additional amount so that those receiving the war veterans allowance would have an actual increase in that allowance as well as
War Veterans
the increase in the old age security and guaranteed income supplement. I hope that something will yet be done about this. When we get the bill to amend the Pension Act back before the committee, perhaps we can have further discussion about this as well.
I support those who argue strenuously that the time has come to permit a veteran who has service in the United Kingdom prior to November 12, 1918, to be included for the purpose of the War Veterans Allowance Act. The number of those still around is dwindling. The number of years they will live to enjoy, if that is the proper word, these sums of money cannot be great. I hope this change can yet be made.
I agree with those who, when the minister was speaking, protested that all he could say about those who live outside of Canada, in the United Kingdom for example, and cannot draw the allowance unless they have the 12 months back in Canada, was that this is under review. After all these years, that is hardly good enough.
I hope the minister will take a further look at these various matters that relate to the war veterans allowance. In earlier speeches, I had something to say about the different ceilings that apply, depending on whether one is under or over 65 and whether he is single or married. All of this could be avoided if we just established a new higher set of ceilings for veterans under the War Veterans Allowance Act.
I see that it is almost one o'clock. I will try to complete my remarks now so that others may speak this afternoon. I leave to my colleague, the hon. member for Timiskaming, a discussion of the Veterans Land Act. The veterans who write to me know all about the rationale of the act. But I support their contention that because they fought for this land, surely they are entitled to purchase a little bit of it. The argument that it is only for those who make their living in agriculture does not stand up any longer.
With regard to the review of cases of veterans of World War I and World War II, I strongly urge that there be much more liberal interpretations by the Canadian Pension Commission of the benefit of the doubt clause.
In conclusion, may I say that veterans, especially those of World War I, should not have to face any more questions. There should be a level of income guaranteed to them. As far as I am concerned, the age of eligibility for this guaranteed income should be lowered. The place to start is by saying to our veterans, you have earned an income and it should be guaranteed to you. I hope the idea of a guaranteed income for veterans will be considered. But I end, Mr. Speaker, where I started. I hope the result of this debate today will lead to what I believe is its main purpose, that it will support the minister in his efforts to get his bill to amend the Pension Act through the cabinet with which he is associated and into this House not later than the end of next week.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO IMPROVE PENSIONS AND REMOVE INJUSTICES TO WAR VETERANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, speaking of veterans, often leads us to think of Canadian history and particularly that of the last thirty years, during which our armed forces have served in the Second World War and the Korean War.
This House must show the greatest concern for these men who have risked their lives in the defence of our country, to enable freedom to survive.
Particularly during the Second World War, even though grudgingly at times, Canadian troops helped to overthrow the Nazi regime, to prevent it from spreading, and carried out great military exploits which should be born in mind when we talk of these problems. The House must show constant concern for veterans, and also continue to shoulder its responsibilities to them.
In our every day life, we come across people who, for lack of work or luck, live in poverty or have other problems. But when veterans are in difficulties, we must recognize that we are somewhat to blame for it.
I therefore hope that the Progressive Conservatives did not introduce this motion on an allotted day in order to make political capital out of the veterans, or just as a way of attracting attention to themselves.
I mentioned the Second World War and the Korean War; we must also remember the peace missions throughout the world in which Canada has given a good account of herself. She has built a good reputation for herself throughout the world.
Therefore, it is a very important duty to look after the interests of those persons and to assume our responsibilities towards them.
Recently, I received a phone call from the wife of a veteran who asked me to help her to obtain for her husband the pension he was entitled to. he was a man who became disabled as a result of his military service, who suffered from gout and who seemed to have been forgotten by the departmental authorities.
Therefore, I lost no time in helping him and in submitting the required representations for that person to obtain justice. It is a fact that those persons are unfairly treated and, as I said earlier, our first responsibility is to ensure that those injustices no longer exist. For instance, I feel that the basic pension rate is unfair. At present, those persons are not treated as they ought to be. They are not treated with the respect which should come before everything, according to the policy drawn up here.
That is why, Mr. Speaker, I am asking the government to take all necessary steps, in order that those war veterans know better days, that at last they enjoy the social justice that this government has often held out to us.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO IMPROVE PENSIONS AND REMOVE INJUSTICES TO WAR VETERANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me a great deal of pleasure to give my support to the motion of my colleague the hon. member for

Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall), or perhaps I should say St. Humble-St. George's-St. Barbe. This motion calls upon the government to get on with the job of implementing measures which have the support of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs and of this House. These measures are intended to alleviate the serious and pressing need of those who rallied to the call when Canada threw its resources together behind the massive effort to free a large part of the world from tyranny. Many of those who did answer the call lie in foreign cemeteries, many of those who returned are still in hospitals or confined to wheelchairs or trying to get along on pensions and allowances.
I should like to point out to the House that the motion moved by my colleague cannot be construed as criticism of the manner in which the new Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) is administering his portfolio.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO IMPROVE PENSIONS AND REMOVE INJUSTICES TO WAR VETERANS
speechtext: Not too many bouquets now.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO IMPROVE PENSIONS AND REMOVE INJUSTICES TO WAR VETERANS
speechtext:
I cannot think of any previous minister of veterans affairs at any time in my memory who has been better suited to the task than the present minister. By temperament and by first hand knowledge of the problems facing veterans, on a day to day basis, the minister is exceptionally well qualified to run that department. Those of us who sit with the minister in committee know that he has the interest of the veterans at heart. He served with distinction in World War II. As most of us on the veterans affairs committee are veterans, Mr. Speaker, I think that I can say without fear of contradiction that our committee is the only committee of this House that consistently functions above partisan politics.
Many thousands of veterans across our country are now looking to those who served alongside them, wondering whether or not we will now rally to their cause. If we do not, then there is nowhere else that they can turn. Where else can they go for help if we in parliament turn our backs on them, or even if we decide what we think is reasonable and just for them, and then let the proposals lie on a shelf and gather dust. Obviously this is not good enough. Those of us on the committee, and the many interested and concerned officials of the veterans organizations have spent hundreds of hours studying, debating and revising proposals and recommendations concerning what we should be providing in the way of benefits, pensions, medical care and the other aspects of a total veterans benefit package.
The package has been assembled and approved. I think that we now have a right to ask the present government: what is holding up the implementation of that veterans benefits package? When I have asked that question in the past I have not been able to get an answer. I will continue to ask the question, but my colleagues and I are running out of patience. We want an answer. I cannot help thinking that the answer is available to the government and needs only to be given to this House and to the veterans who are waiting. The main reason I was so anxious to speak on this motion is that I am deeply concerned about the attitude that appears to exist in the Department of Veterans Affairs in respect of the veterans affairs hospital in London, Ontario. The hospital is the Westminster Hos-


pital, and I do not like to think of what is going to happen to this hospital if the government's announced plans are carried out.
To begin with, I must say that I am not in agreement with the policy in the past few years whereby the Department of Veterans Affairs has gradually gone out of the business of providing and maintaining hospitals for veterans' domiciliary care. There has been a tendency to transfer veterans hospitals to provinces and municipalities for operation, reducing the capacity of these hospitals to deal with bedridden veterans. Provinces and municipalities are not, and have never been, in the business of caring for veterans. This is a responsibility of the federal government, and if I had been in parliament when this policy was first introduced, the department would have had a tough time with me. I would have fought it then, and I am quite prepared to fight it now, right down to the wire.
For some time now the federal government has been discussing with the province, and with the city of London, various schemes for the transfer of Westminster Hospital to the province or to the city. Dr. K. S. Ritchie, assistant deputy minister (hospitals) of the Department of Veterans Affairs said in an interview with the London Free Press last month that the real interest of the DVA was to see the Westminster Hospital become part of the community health facility in order that the future care of veterans will be safeguarded. This is a strange statement of principle. On the one hand, the assistant deputy minister expresses concern over the future welfare of veterans who require hospital treatment and care. At the same time, he says that this can best be assured by having the DVA turn the hospital over to another jurisdiction, jurisdiction incidentally that does not have any responsibilities for veterans care.
In addition to the buildings on the site, Westminster Hospital also has a vast parkland area comprising about 342 acres of prime land. In the past, this parkland has been available to veterans who were able to leave their beds and walk around the grounds, or sit and read or whatever they wanted to do, in a tranquil setting. It may well be that there are people in the DVA who feel this is too good for disabled veterans, men and women who have nothing else but this to look forward to for the rest of their lives. I cannot accept a policy that seeks to transfer responsibility for veterans care to any agency or jurisdiction other than that department in which the responsibility has been vested. That agency is the DVA, and I will insist on a better explanation from them as to why they are not disposed to retain that responsibility.
If some change is called for in the administration of Westminster Hospital, and if some new disposition is necessary, then I have a proposal of my own to make. This hospital was built and has been maintained through the years as a veterans facility. It should remain a veterans facility. My proposal is that it should be declared a national monument to those who have served our country, both to those who did not return, and to those who did return but who are destined to spend the remainder of their lives in the care of the veterans administration.
War Veterans
The grounds around the hospital should be preserved intact to serve the veterans who are domiciled in the hospital and also to serve the people in the community. We have other national monuments across our country that are less deserving of the distinction. I can think of no better way to preserve the memory of, and to do honour to, those of our men and women who have served their country in several wars. I will answer the cranks who would say that such a monument would honour war itself by saying to them that if they had served they would know that those who hate war the most are those who have served in one. I venture to say there are people who would fight my proposal with every means at their disposal. That beautiful land which surrounds Westminster must have some councillors and developers in London drooling and dreaming. I daresay that there are people who cannot wait for the Department of Veterans Affairs to divest itself of the hospital so that they may begin their politicking, scheming and manoeuvring.
I can see high rises, town houses and possibly a shopping centre rising almost overnight on those beautiful grounds. Some people might say at this point that the present council in London would preserve the ground and buildings intact, and that they would do their utmost to prevent it falling into the hands of developers. However, councils change and I doubt very seriously that anyone would suggest that the best way to preserve it as it is would be to have the Department of Veterans Affairs turn it over to someone else. I do not have any more faith in the province in this respect than I would have in any other political jurisdiction. The province does not have responsibility for the care of veterans. I do not believe it would be very long before the provincial government would decide that this area is too prime and too expensive to maintain, and would take steps to enhance the utility and the income potential of this facility.
There is only one way the future of Westminster can be assured as a veterans facility. That is by making it a monument as well as a continuing institution to provide domicilary care for veterans. The designation of Westminster as a national monument would not preclude or prevent its use in other ways. In fact, if it were established as a continuing facility under the patronage of the federal government many additional programs could be developed for the hospital. For instance, there is no reason that portions of the hospital not required for veterans could not be utilized for other patients. London needs additional beds for children's care. This might be the answer to the problem for some time to come. A hospital such as Westminster would be ideally suited to the new role of a medical teaching facility in both pure and applied research as well as the training of doctors who want to upgrade their proficiency in specialized areas of medicine. In fact, if it could be established now that Westminster would continue in perpetuity as a medical facility with the primary function of ensuring domiciliary care for veterans, any number of additional uses might be made of these facilities through the years.
There is a possibility that we will be able to avoid becoming involved in any future wars. This is the fervent hope of all responsible people. In that event there will
26314-31}


War Veterans
come a time when there will not be any need for veterans hospitals as such. However, that time has not arrived, and we have a solemn responsibility to maintain sufficient facilities for the care of our veterans. We cannot slough off that responsibility to anyone else, however well-meaning they might be.
There are some other aspects of veterans care and benefits on which I planned to speak, but I felt I had to make my point with regard to veterans hospitals in general and Westminster hospital in particular. I should like to mention I am a bit disturbed about the apparent lack of real interest on the part of the government in extending the deadline on such an important program as the Veterans Land Act. This act has been a Godsend to the many thousands of returned veterans. Many members have spoken on this subject, but there is one area on which I should like to touch. There are approximately 200 to 300 persons who would qualify under the Veterans' Land Act who are still in the armed forces. When these people leave the armed forces, they must state the area in which they would like to build. If they have not done so by March 31, 1974 they will have to designate a province in which within seven or eight years they might wish to build. I would like to say that the department should extend the program just for that reason alone.
There is another area which is of great concern to me. I have risen twice in this House to seek the unanimous consent of the House to have immediate citizenship granted to war veterans who are honourably discharged from the armed forces. I did not receive such unanimous consent, and I can only assume the reason I did not receive it is that the same people who did not give the consent are the people who are holding up the passage of this bill. There is no reason in the world that we cannot grant at least citizenship to men who fought in the armed forces of this country, not necessarily on request but by right.
On a final note, I would urge the cabinet or whoever is holding up implementation of the benefit package we have approved to turn it loose and let it carry through to Royal Assent. It does not do anybody any good so long as it stays on the shelf. If our troops had discharged their responsibility in combat as loosely and as cavalierly as we seem to be regarding this latest benefit legislation, I shudder to think who would be running our country today. We certainly would not be.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO IMPROVE PENSIONS AND REMOVE INJUSTICES TO WAR VETERANS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak briefly on the subject of veterans affairs. I am concerned lest our veterans suffer from the political competition that is a normal way of life in this House. As the proposer of the motion admits, committee discussion of veterans business is mostly non-partisan. I should like our House discussion also to be kept on the same plane. The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands suggested the motive behind the motion which is before the House. I agree with him, but I also suggest that this member's motivation in applying pressure to the minister and to the government in this manner is to drive in the thin edge of the wedge leading to future promotion of his socialistic theories.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO IMPROVE PENSIONS AND REMOVE INJUSTICES TO WAR VETERANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on a point of order. I do not mind being accused of driving

in the thin edge of the wedge, but I should like to be identified as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO IMPROVE PENSIONS AND REMOVE INJUSTICES TO WAR VETERANS
speechtext:
I offer my sincere apology to the hon. member. I do not believe that such an objective should be a consideration in this debate. As the vice-chairman of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs, I have been pleased to see the unanimity of the members representing all parties in safeguarding and promoting the interests of our veterans. I believe we will achieve our joint objective by emphasizing the very special needs and rights of our veterans and their families.
There is one other point I should like to make which is of somewhat local character. It concerns the veterans hospitals in the province of Quebec and the program to transfer these hospitals, along with other veterans hospitals, to provincial jurisdiction in the future. I wish to make the point that the responsibility for the care of our veterans is 100 per cent a federal responsibility and in this respect, until we are sure that these rights and the wishes of our veterans will be looked after to the degree to which we, the federal representatives, want to see them looked after, we should not pursue such a transfer. Also, we must respect the rights of the veterans to have a very strong voice in this decision to transfer their hospitals to another jurisdiction. While there are a number of statutes and regulations contained in what we refer to as the Veterans Charter, I would like to deal at this time with the War Veterans Allowance Act and Part XI of the Civilian War Pensions and Allowances Act.
The War Veterans Allowance Act is that part of the Veterans Charter designed to ensure that those whose wartime service meets the requirements of the act shall, in spite of advanced age or incapacity, be assured of an income. This is attained by providing an allowance on a modified income test basis which ensures that the income of a veteran, his widow or orphans, does not fall below the amounts set out in the schedule of the act. We are deeply conscious of the debt we owe to those men and women who risked their lives in the interests of preserving Canada's freedom. This government has been alert to the needs of this important group of Canadian citizens and has taken a number of steps to assure them of a better standard of living.
On March 21, 1972 the regulations were amended to remove the four months restriction on casual employment. The result of this action was that the length of the employment ceased to be a factor and the dollar value of the earnings became the only yardstick to be applied. On May 15, 1972, we exempted the cost of living increases in the old age security and guaranteed income supplement monthly payments amounting to $15 for single recipients and $30 for married recipients. By doing this, the government ensures that those recipients aged 65 and over would receive an OAS/GIS increase and not have their allowances reduced by a like amount.
On May 19, 1972, we amended the War Veterans Allowance Act to provide for escalation of the rates and ceilings effective January 1, 1972, and on January 1 of each succeeding year in accordance with increases in the consumer price index. As a result of this, war veterans allowance


and civilian war allowances recipients will no longer have to wait and hope for an increase, wondering when it will happen and how much it will be. They now know that if the cost of living goes up, so will their allowances and income ceilings.
On November 9, 1972 the regulations were amended so that the value of a home in excess of $10,000 would no longer cause a reduction in the allowance paid each month. This was a great help to people whose homes had escalated in value. Before the regulations were changed, they did suffer a loss of income because of the increased values in real estate.
On January 13, 1973 the amount of casual earnings permitted in any allowance year was increased from $800 to $1,000 for single recipients, and from $1,200 to $1,500 for married recipients. This is one of the provisions of the War Veterans Allowance Act and Civilian War Allowances Act which help to make them outstanding pieces of legislation of which we should all be proud. While unfortunately all recipients are not able to avail themselves of this exemption, it is beneficial for those who can. The result of this change is that, in the absence of any other income, a single recipient can have a monthly allowance of $151.14 and earn $1,480 a year, for a total of $3,293.68 a year. Married recipients can have a monthly allowance of $257.21 and earn $2,340 a year for a total income of $5,426.52.
The War Veterans Allowance Act and Part XI of the Civilian War Pensions and Allowances Act are two very important parts of the Veterans Charter. Bill C-148, as all hon. members know, increased the rates in the War Veterans Allowance Act and the Civilian War Allowances Act by $20.14 for single recipients and $39.60 for married recipients. The War Veterans Allowance Act and the Civilian War Pensions and allowances Act rates have been increased by $30.14 a month or 24.8 per cent for single recipients and $56.21 a month or 27.8 per cent for married recipients since December 31, 1971. The rates for orphans have similarly been increased by more than 24 per cent during the same period.
Like all hon. members, I was pleased to see the rates and ceilings increased twice this year, once on January 1 and again on April 1. I was especially pleased, however, at the amendment to the act which removed for all time the restriction on personal property which, prior to April 1 of this year, was limited to $1,250 for single recipients and $2,500 for those who are married. As a result of the removal of the personal property limitations, the War Veterans Allowance Act and the Civilian War Pensions and Allowances Act, which were previously geared to a means test, are now geared to a modified income test.
There can be no doubt that the previous restriction caused a great deal of frustration and sadness on the part of many applicants and recipients. I have had letters from widows whose husbands had been receiving the war veterans allowance or civilian war allowances during their lifetime. The veteran died and left his wife $5,000 in insurance. No matter how old or crippled she was, until she reduced her insurance money to the permissible limit through ordinary maintenance, she was automatically ineligible for an allowance. In other cases, a recipient might receive a small inheritance and because the amount of personal property was then more than was allowed, that
War Veterans
recipient would lose his allowance and possibly be faced with a recoverable overpayment. This particular amendment is a milestone in veterans legislation and will be beneficial to hundreds of recipients and applicants. I understand that last year alone 1,375 recipients had their allowance cancelled because their personal property increased over the legal amount. In many cases the excess was small, but the result was the same.
I am sure that all hon. members will agree that it is right that we should be constantly on the alert for ways to improve the legislation which affects our veterans and their dependants. I believe that the government has demonstrated that awareness and its willingness to take the legislative action necessary to bring about the desired improvements. These improvements, together with the abolition of the restriction on personal property holdings effective April 1, 1973, are concrete evidence of this government's determination to honour our debt to those who served Canada in her hour of need.
In conclusion, I want to add a word of praise of what our Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) has been attempting to do in his short term in this House. I advise hon. members that he is giving his weekend to the veterans, as he has done with so many weekends. He leaves by plane after this debate is concluded this afternoon to attend the Quebec legion convention at Ste Anne de Bellevue. He will be visiting Ste Anne de Bellevue veterans hospital tomorrow morning, and then he will fly out again to repeat the same process in Ontario. I feel that while veterans affairs are in the good hands of our present minister our veterans need have no fear that they will not be given a fair deal in the legislation which all members of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs are anxious to see before the House.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO IMPROVE PENSIONS AND REMOVE INJUSTICES TO WAR VETERANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the first in need of our consideration are the last to be served in this session of parliament. Most of those on a government pension have had an increase established for them in this session of parliament, except the disabled war veterans. A parliamentary committee representing all parties has agreed on the need, and has agreed on the extent of what the increase should be. All parties are agreed on the necessity to make the increase as soon as possible.
The Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) indicated that legislation for the increase was to be brought to the House before the Easter recess. There is now an indication from the same minister that the legislation will be brought to the House before the end of May. There was also an indication from the House leader of the Liberal party that, hopefully, it would be brought to the House before the summer recess. Therefore, the hold up must be in the cabinet. It is easy in opposition to criticize; it is easy in opposition to say what should be done; it is easy in opposition to promise everything, because in opposition one doesn't have the responsibility for acting.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO IMPROVE PENSIONS AND REMOVE INJUSTICES TO WAR VETERANS
speechtext: Which side are you on?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO IMPROVE PENSIONS AND REMOVE INJUSTICES TO WAR VETERANS
speechtext:
On the side of the DVA, as I hope you are. In opposition one is unhindered by the final responsibility, by the final formula. When one does not have the responsi-


War Veterans
bility, some of the complexities and complications are unknown. A government cannot immediately and always live up to its good intentions. But granted all that, Mr. Speaker, the government should move, because it must move to save the dignity and the peace of mind of those now on inadequate pensions.
Those who have given more than most are getting less than most. More than any, we are subjecting them to the torture of the government's indecision. The disabled, most of whom are denied a life of activity, have more time to think, have more time to be concerned, have more time to be dismayed. No matter what the complexities and the complications of coming through with a formula, the necessity of action now is so great that the government should make it a priority item.
The House has been spending more time in sympathy with the murderers of our society than with those in society who sacrificed to make our society safe for all. Let us get our priorities straight, and with the urgency of an emergency measure let the government act no later than next week to bring in the legislation, to bring justice to our disabled war veterans, to end the uncertainty and the real anguish as they wait from day to day. We cannot solve all the problems of the world or all the problems of the nation, but the government does have the wherewithal to serve the modest needs of the disabled war veteran.
Let the government have the determination. Let not grandiose plans for the future blind us to the practical needs of today. It is not that the disabled war veterans situation is going to result in measures which will cost the government hundreds of millions of dollars. There are not that many survivors of our wars. We, in Canada, have not been directly involved in a major war since Korea. We do not have the problem of a continuing number of disability cases. We have a situation where we are in debt to a small group of men, in debt for a very long time, and the need now is for immediate action in establishing the new basic rate for those on the war disability pension.

speakeroldname: Mr. Joseph-Philippe Guay (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO IMPROVE PENSIONS AND REMOVE INJUSTICES TO WAR VETERANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I, too, would like to speak briefly on behalf of the veterans with respect to the motion that is before us today. I would like to bring to the attention of the House that, from time to time since last autumn, mention has been made of a possible increase in pensions paid under the Pension Act to veterans who suffered a disability related to military service, and to dependents in the event of their death.
I think it is important to note that the veterans are not just asking for an increase in pension rates. Rather, they seek a base rate of pension tied to one or more groups in the private or public sector. Hon. members will recall that the recommendations contained in the joint report by representatives of the veterans' organizations and officials of the Department of Veterans Affairs and the Pension Commission, were endorsed by the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs some time ago. Those of us who were on that committee will recall that five categories in the public service were selected as representative of unskilled labour, a level acceptable to the veterans' spokesmen. Veterans tell me that the principle of finding a firm base for the rate of pension is at this point in time even more important than an increase in dollars. I understand that
[Mr. Arrol.l
the matter is now under close study by the cabinet, and the House leader has stated that we can expect a bill before the House before the end of June.
