speechtext:
I also would like that. I did not say that the legislation will not arrive in May. I said it certainly would come before the end of June, and if by chance the House leader brings it in within the next few days I will be most happy. I am sure that the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) feels the same way as we do. I am sure that the minister wants to accelerate introduction of the legislation and have it approved as soon as possible. The vice-chairman of the standing committee has expressed his feelings about the minister. What he said was worth while hearing. I know he meant it. I, too, know the dedication which the minister has brought to his job ever since taking over the department. He deserves to be complimented. It is not every minister who will do the work that he does every weekend. It shows his concern for the veterans.
The veterans' organizations also asked for a standard formula, fixing the ratio on a firm percentage basis, to cover the additional pension paid to a veteran on behalf of his wife and child or children. Similarly, it was felt that the same basis should be provided for setting the rate of pension paid to a widow. Historically, an increase in disability pension was announced from time to time, but the percentage increase varied as did the ratio of additional pensions paid for dependants. There would seem to be some merit in the proposals put forward for many years by the veterans groups who have held that an increase in the basic rate when implemented should be measured against some point of reference.
This matter has now been successively before a study group, the standing committee and the government for almost a year, and has obviously been carefully analysed by all concerned. I share the hope of other hon. members that further information on this subject will soon be forthcoming.
Over the past year, most hon. members will have received letters from war veterans or their dependants seeking assistance in urging the Canadian Pension Commission to act on pension applications. I must confess I was shocked to learn only recently that as of April 24 last year the commission was faced with a backlog of 8,975 applications for a basic award, and I understand this does not include many ancillary benefits, including pensions for wives and children.
I have done a bit of research and was referred to a national magazine called The Fragment, put out by the War Amps of Canada. This magazine contains an article dealing with delays by the Pension Commission in granting pension awards, and points out all is not black or white. I will repeat that, Mr. Speaker: it points out that all


is not black or white. For example, one must realize it is now 28 years since the end of World War II and while there have been other brush-fire wars, the bulk of the claims outstanding relate to the 1939-1945 conflict. Most of the so-called routine claims from World War II have long since been granted; it is the difficult claims that require a great deal of research. In many cases, there is no intermediate medical report between 1945 and the death of a veteran in 1973. The widow may feel that her husband's fatal heart attack related to his arduous service in a battle area and submit a claim. One can readily understand the correspondence required by the commission, the bureau of pensions advocates, if involved in the case, and frequently a veterans' organization, in seeking records of medical treatment since 1945 and in seeking witnesses who may be able to support the widow's claim that her husband's health was not good over the many years since service.
I think it is of interest to note that since the amendments of March 30, 1971, a widow may claim an award in respect of a condition for which her husband neglected to claim during his lifetime. One need hardly mention the difficulties involved in this exercise, especially since the veteran is now out of the picture and there may be only meagre evidence, if any, in support of the claim.
Many of the claims advanced recently are not new. Hon. members are aware that the amendments to the Pension Act of March 1971 provided for an open door policy to all. This means that in addition to the many new measures introduced, any veteran whose claim to pension since 1918 was not granted is afforded an opportunity of starting over again. It will be readily apparent that a claim that has been aggressively prosecuted on a number of occasions over the past 35 years, has collected many volumes, and all this data again be reviewed if the claim is to receive the attention it deserves.
One must ask, then, what steps are now being taken to deal with the backlog? I find there has been a marked increase in the staff of the commission since April, 1971- indeed the total staff figure now stands at 359, an increase of 14 per cent over the past two years. In addition, hon. members will recall a bill was before the House last July to authorize an increase in the size of the commission to 24 members. Immediate steps led to the appointment of seven new members and, although I am advised a lengthy training period is essential, the new members will play a decisive role in reducing the backlog. In this regard, the chairman of the commission has recently stated he feels the corner has been turned, and since January of this year output is increasing and the number of claims pending has been reduced on successive months. He has cautioned, however, there will likely be surges from time to time, thus requiring constant review of methods to speed up the adjudication process.
To sum up, I am satisfied the officials of the commission are doing their best, but at the moment it is not quite good enough. Hon. members will, I am sure, join me when I suggest no concerned person in the Pension Commission can rest easy until every veteran's claim has received the attention it deserves.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to bring to the attention of members of this House the fact that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) who
War Veterans
for many years has participated on the Veterans Affairs Committee and in fact has always spoken about the various pension boards and commissions, who has dedicated almost all his life to the benefit of people who should rightly receive pensions, who sits opposite me but whom I have always recognized for the work he has done-that hon. gentleman will be 65 years young on June 18. I feel I should bring this to the attention of the House. At that time he will be eligible for the $100 a month pension through what he often refers to as the OAP, old age pension. All members of the House I am sure will want to wish him many more years of active life, health and happiness in doing what he is doing for the benefit of all Canadians.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO IMPROVE PENSIONS AND REMOVE INJUSTICES TO WAR VETERANS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO IMPROVE PENSIONS AND REMOVE INJUSTICES TO WAR VETERANS
speechtext:
Therefore, it is only going to be another day in a long and illustrious career of fighting for pensioners. However, I do appreciate the words of the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Guay) in relation to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. I believe that, in relation to this subject, that appreciation should be extended to most members with whom I have had the opportunity of sitting for 15 years. The hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) who was vice-chairman of that committee, a fact of which I was not aware, started out by saying how terrible it was to raise this question. He condemned the hon. member for bringing it forward, and other hon. members for having endorsed the hon. member's position. He went on to say how wonderful the government has been to our veterans in paying the veterans allowances, not understanding that these only apply to people who are totally disabled and below the age of 60. If they are over 60, they have to pass a means test. That legislation does not apply to them if they are over 65, as those veterans are to get benefits from increased old age pensions and other old age assistance.
Therefore, his remarks were not in keeping with what has been happening for a long time in the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs. The members of that commit-


War Veterans
tee are anxious, on behalf of all veterans in this country, to see the best possible type of veterans charter and legislation adopted. I think the minister would be the first to agree that in thus raising this issue the House is putting its weight behind the proposition that in this country there is general acceptance of the idea that the basic rate for disability pensions should be calculated by taking the average of wages paid for five junior categories in the civil service. This is a change in concept, and members of the opposition consider this so important that they wish to add their support to any application the minister might make to cabinet for such a substantial change.
When I first was a member of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs, I believe 15 or 16 years ago, the base rate mentioned was to be tied to the rate paid to sweepers, cleaners and similar categories in the civil service. This decision was made by a committee following the First World War on the ground that such categories ranked lowest in the federal civil service. It was felt that if a veteran was totally disabled he ought to get as much as if he were digging ditches or sweeping floors for the federal government. Everybody agreed. The only disagreement was over how one was to establish that concept. In the meantime, the sweeper has departed; the job of ditch-digger in the civil service has disappeared. Those categories were referred to but have not existed for some time. Therefore, the government has arbitrarily set a level of benefits from time to time that has not met a criterion that the veterans themselves believe to be fair and reasonable.
Certainly that was the opinion of the special joint study group that looked into this matter. The amount that group decided on is not large. It took into consideration payments such as income tax that would normally be made by civil servants in the course of their employment. The figure arrived at is, in my opinion, reasonable and will be applicable not only this year and next year but for as long as veterans depend on this type of pension. That, of course, will be for as long as there are surviving veterans from the Second World War and the Korean war.
I think the criterion arrived at is almost ideal. The determination of the basic rate will not be tied to the wages paid to a single category in the civil service. It will be tied to the average wage paid to five categories. It seems to me that so long as we stick to five categories, any one of which may fluctuate up or down but all five of which will be taken on average, we shall be dealing with this problem in a fair and reasonable way. I am surprised that the vice-chairman of the veterans affairs committee did not understand that the committee was totally in favour of that proposition and endorsed it almost without debate. This raises the question of whether we should do these things without debate. We thought everybody understood this position. We were of the opinion that everybody taking part in the debate today would not criticize the government but would support the proposition that the government should take this course of action. Perhaps, for the benefit of newer members, there should be more explanation of the subject. I think, nevertheless, that we would all come to exactly the same position as we now espouse.
The member who moved this motion today did not do so to embarrass the government. He did not move it as a

non-confidence motion. His purpose in moving it was totally different. His purpose was to enable us in opposition parties to lend support, publicly, to the minister and to the committee so that the government and other members may have the benefit of opinions expressed in the committee and a decision on this question can be taken as soon as possible. He wanted to bring this matter to the attention of ministers and others who must make the final decision on matters affecting veterans. He did not move his motion for the purpose of getting any advantage from it, or for criticizing the government.
I want to raise a second point touched on by most speakers, that is, concerning the difficulty we are experiencing with a limited number of veterans who are reaching retirement age or are considering retirement and who want to move from the area in which they may have worked for a number of years to an area in which they can retire. These veterans wish to take advantage of the Veterans Land Act provisions which will allow them to buy a piece of land and build a small house-and under the terms of the VLA it will be a very small house in most areas! At any rate, they will be able to build a small house.
For the sake of those members who, like the vice-chairman of the committee, may not understand exactly what we have been talking about, let me explain that after the war three forms of help outside of the normal veterans' assistance were given to veterans. They were given reestablishment allowances which were not exceedingly large. I think the amount was usually under $1,000, depending on the number of months of service. Second, they were given the benefit of the university and retraining program. In many cases these benefits were extensive. I took advantage of that particular program.
The third form of help was given under the Veterans Land Act. Many farmers were re-established under the Veterans Land Act, others were established on smaller pieces of land under the smallholding provisions of the VLA. These holdings varied from two acres to approximately half an acre. Concessions were made to those holding even half an acre if the veteran was 50 per cent disabled. Also, that small piece of land could be fairly close to another piece on which he might build. In other words, the land did not all need to be in one block but all the pieces had to be reasonably close to one another.
It was decided in 1964-and I think it is safe to say the committee really did not put up much of a fuss-that 1974 was to be the cut-off date for building under the Veterans Land Act provisions. Most of us were thinking in terms of farmers and of the age of veterans. We were also thinking, when making that decision, that the final cut-off date was ten years away. Those ten years have gone awfully fast and we are rapidly approaching 1974, the final cut-off date for building. Many veterans really do not consider the smallholding provisions until they are about to retire. I have received a considerable number of letters from veterans in the past two or three weeks. These people are much better informed about the March, 1974, cut-off date than they are about the fact that they should have a certificate of qualification issued before October, 1968, in order to qualify under the Veterans Land Act.


I am asking that we extend this provision and eliminate the qualification date. Under the smallholdings section a veteran was able to obtain up to $18,000 under the Veterans Land Act for acquiring land and building a home. Of this amount $6,000 was at 3.5 per cent interest. Therein lies the advantage of the smallholding legislation. The remaining provision and advantages are involved in the repayment program. If the repayment was completed there were other built-in advantages amounting to about $1,500. In my opinion, there is no justification in cutting off the Veterans Land Act as far as it affects smallholdings. I do not want to see a farmer saddled with an operation from which he has to make a living and make payments at an advanced age, but the letters I receive with regard to smallholdings indicate a number of problems.
One of my colleagues showed me a letter the other day which he received from a person who has lived in Yellowknife since the war. That city is quite northerly and I presume this man does not want to stay there for the rest of his life. He has some savings and now wants to take advantage of the smallholding section of the Veterans Land Act and move to British Columbia. He said he did not know about the qualifying date, and I believe him. Therefore, he cannot take advantage of the Veterans Land Act. He also said he has not been able to take advantage of other sections. But if the record is checked I think it will probably be found that he did receive credits which will now have to be repaid. After 30 years, a person's memory sometimes tends to be faulty. This is not an insurmountable obstacle. That money could be repaid in order to take advantage of the qualification provisions.
I received a letter from one of my constituents who had received a re-establishment credit in 1954 of $270. After repaying his re-establishment credit he qualified under the smallholding section. He looked around for a suitable property but was unable to find one. When he notified the department that he was unable to find a suitable property he was refunded his re-establishment credit. He lost his certificate of qualification because he drew his re-establishment credit for the second time. Obviously, this man has qualified. Even though the qualification was withdrawn, I suggest that he is still qualified regardless of the fact that he gave up his certificate.
If the members of this House really believe the veteran has the right to take advantage of the Veterans Land Act, they will do three things to make it worth while. First, they will have to convince the minister and his officials that it is necessary to wipe out the qualifying date, at least with regard to smallholdings. I am sure that would be difficult for the minister to do. When I asked the minister if he would settle for ministerial discretion he said, "In no way." I do not blame him. If we are going to do this, I do not see why we should load all our problems on the minister and he should have to make the decisions. I think it should just be withdrawn.
Second, in order to be fair to someone living in an urban community I think the $18,000 restriction should be changed. It is unreasonable. In the Toronto Star the other day a lot for a house was advertised at $18,000. The lot was on the edge of a ravine which had not been filled. I am not sure whether the ravine would have to be filled before
War Veterans
building, but after paying $18,000 for the lot there would not be much left for the tent he would have to put on it. A much more reasonable qualification would be $25,000, considering the change in land value in urban areas.
Third, if we are going to make this change we should also change that which is bothering the minister and his department, namely, the administration section in the Veterans Land Act. This smallholding section, including the terms and regulations, should be turned over to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation or the Farm Credit Corporation for administration. There is really no justification for duplicating the administrative costs. The amount being spent on the Veterans Land Act program is not being increased but the per unit administrative costs are rising quite steeply. Despite what the vice-chairman of the committee says, we should make these kinds of suggestions. If they have the support of all members of this House, particularly in a minority government situation, they should receive consideration, because we are not necessarily dealing with a costly item.
The minister and the committee should give serious consideration to eliminating the qualification date of October, 1968, as well as eliminating the commencement of construction date of March, 1974, which is rapidly approaching. All veterans should have an equal right in making their own decision. This qualifying date eliminates that right for those who were not in a position to take advantage of this program ten years ago but are in that position today. If they are now in such a position we should make these advantages available to them.
In view of the service these veterans gave to our country they should be entitled to a 3!/2 per cent interest rate on the first $6,000. The balance would be at CMHC rates. If administration is the costly item, it should be taken over by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. If we do this we will be making a contribution to the welfare of the veterans of our country.
I hope the minister conveys to the cabinet and Treasury Board the support he has received from the opposition by using one of their opposition days for the veterans of Canada. I hope the minister can convince the cabinet that the proposal, particularly with regard to war veterans pensions, is reasonable, just and supported by all members of this House.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO IMPROVE PENSIONS AND REMOVE INJUSTICES TO WAR VETERANS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO IMPROVE PENSIONS AND REMOVE INJUSTICES TO WAR VETERANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I cannot tell you how pleased I am to be able to contribute to this debate. I was pleased to be a member of the veterans affairs committee. Most of us have only one thought, and that is to make a unanimous decision about the proper treatment of veterans as far as pensions are concerned. At present there seems to be one little snag, but I believe this will be overcome shortly.
All hon. members have been concerned about the availability of medical treatment for veterans. There are still about 900,000 veterans in Canada. In all quarters of the House, arrangements for their medical care are held to be of first importance. The amount of time devoted to treatment of members of the armed services by the Department
3934


War Veterans
of Veterans Affairs amounts to 10,455 man-years annually. However, only about 20 per cent of the expenditures of the department are used for this purpose. It should be pointed out, also, that some of this expenditure is recoverable through provincial insurance plans.
After the First World War treatment services and hospitals were set up. Some treatment was, of course, carried out in civilian hospitals and by private doctors. At the present time, diagnostic and other treatment is available to recipients of war veterans allowances. I think most of those benefiting from these services have been fairly generously treated; at least, that has been the case in my experience and I believe most hon. members share this view.
However, the department also looks after current members of the armed forces, members of the RCMP and others in the public service, so the department has to administer about 5,000 beds in eight veterans hospitals in addition to 364 beds in three veterans homes. There is also some contracting-out of veterans care to university centres, especially in cases where hospitals have been turned over to the community. I saw some of this work in Sunny-brook hospital. It became fairly obvious that, taking account of the diminishing number of chronically ill or wounded, people who had succumbed to the advances of age or to their wounds, the treatment of veterans became concentrated on those with acute illnesses and that to carry on highly organized and beautifully equipped hospitals for veterans, when their numbers did not fill those hospitals, was both uneconomic and undesirable.
Moreover, we think very strongly that veterans should be given the very best treatment available; they need a high quality of care such as is available in community general hospitals and university teaching hospitals. For this reason there has been a change of emphasis in the type of treatment carried out. Since 1968 there has been a reduction of 12 per cent in the use made of hospital services on a patient-day basis.
As hon. members have pointed out, we have been very lucky, or blessed, because we have had no new wars to contend with. The number of veterans requiring chronic patient care is decreasing all the time, and we ought now to move in the direction of providing the required service to an increasing extent by reserving beds in community general hospitals. What worries most hon. members who are interested in the welfare of veterans is the feeling that some of the old, well-known hospitals have been graded down by being turned into community hospitals. I have mentioned Sunnybrook hospital. There is the hospital in Ste. Foy, Quebec, and there is the Lancaster hospital in Saint John, New Brunswick. These three institutions have been transferred. I do not think the problems mentioned by the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Beattie) are insoluble. Since one of my hon. friends may well be speaking about that aspect of the question, I shall not mention it further.
The implementation of hospital and medical care insurance plans by provincial governments is having an effect upon the occupancy rate of veterans hospitals, and we shall have to accept the situation. A high proportion of veterans are now insured under provincial plans so the cost of their medical treatment is recoverable from the
[Mr. Railton.l
province. Again, now that veterans are insured, many of them choose to enter hospitals near their own homes. This results in more vacant beds being left in the veterans hospitals.
In many instances the provinces realize that they already have a major responsibility for the operation of veterans hospitals. Increasing emphasis on regional health planning has encouraged the provinces to reassess the unused assets represented by facilities in veterans hospitals. Throughout negotiations the department has not neglected its responsibilities to veterans. It has intensified programs for the modernization of equipment and accommodation, ensuring adequate treatment and facilities for veterans and assisting in the retention of essential professional services.
Negotiations for the transfer of Deer Lodge hospital, Winnipeg, are nearing completion and they have recently been initiated for Westminster hospital, London. It is also understood that discussions with the provinces appear favourable toward the initiation of negotiations for the transfer of Camp Hill hospital, Halifax; Queen Mary veterans hospital, Montreal; Ste Anne's hospital, Ste Anne de Bellevue; Rideau veterans home, Ottawa; Colonel Belcher hospital, Calgary; Shaughnessy hospital, Vancouver; and Veterans hospital, Victoria. Although it is evident that the transfer of veterans hospitals may not be completed by the original target year of 1973-74, there is promise that it may not be delayed too long after next year.
I thank hon. members for allowing me to speak today. I want to add my felicitations to those of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) in respect of the minister, for his superb handling of his ministry.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO IMPROVE PENSIONS AND REMOVE INJUSTICES TO WAR VETERANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to speak to this motion because I believe this parliament should do everything possible to speed benefits for war veterans as unanimously recommended by the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs. I am sure representations have been made in the past year regarding the basic rate of pensions and the inequities of the system, particularly with the inflationary trend. I am sure persons making those representations on behalf of veterans have been told that a joint study group has prepared a report and that we must await the report before we can recommend to cabinet any changes in the present system.
The report has been submitted to and unanimously accepted by the standing committee of this House, and I am sure the speed at which the matter was passed through the committee must have established a record. There was not one dissenting vote. Everyone who spoke said he did not want to hold up the recommendations a moment longer than necessary. We did not even hear all the witnesses who planned to plead the case for war veterans. Newspapers, veterans' organizations and veterans' magazines all praised those who contributed to the study.
Many of us will recall reading newspaper headlines at the time the report went through, some of which were "Pension plan moves quickly", "Basic pension rate recommendations favoured", "Break for veterans", "New regula-


tions for the burnt-out pensioner", "Ottawa moves to raise pension of war veterans". Then came the one that caused some of us to raise our eyebrows, "New veterans pension plan encounters hurdles in cabinet". We were a little bit disturbed on reading that.
The minister is regarded highly by all members of the standing committee. We applauded his statement on the introduction of the joint study report and I am sure we all felt it would be a simple "a-b-c" matter when dealt with by the cabinet, but apparently this was not the case. I thought this year we had made a breakthrough, but with the delay in cabinet I expect we will be told that the recommendations will be changed or shelved. I am very disturbed about that prospect. Emotions run high when this sort of thing happens, especially when we think of the millions of dollars we pour into useless LIP programs; how some of the industry, trade and commerce people toss off a few million dollars to an industry group and say it was a calculated risk or that we are gaining experience in this field.
The Department of National Health and Welfare is pushing for more social increases; and one remembers that time in the past year when we paid out $1.5 billion in unemployment insurance benefits because of poor economic planning and forecasting. Yet now we find the government holding back on increases in veterans pensions. What group of people deserves more consideration than our war veterans? We will, with great fanfare, give millions of dollars in grants to emerging nations and rush to the aid of victims of national disasters in other countries and justify our gifts on humanitarian grounds, but what group in society needs more help than our war veterans?
I was somewhat embarrassed a few weeks ago when I participated in a celebration in memory of the battle of the Atlantic. It was a ceremony to commemorate those who died in that battle during World War II, involving the placing of wreaths by various veterans' groups, the municipality and the province of Ontario on the Cenotaph. It was discovered that the person representing the Department of National Defence had no wreath. I was contacted and I ordered a wreath comparable to those of the province and the municipality. I was later informed by the department that this was not an allowable expense. It is not the dollar amount which bothers me, as that is not important as far as I am concerned; it is the principle involved. I find it incredible that this government would not pay for a wreath to commemorate those who gave their lives in defence of their country.
The minister made reference to the aims and purposes of the Veterans Land Act. Like other members who have spoken, I have had many persons from veterans' organizations, legions and clubs speak to me about this act. We all recognize the original intent, but times and conditions have changed and the desires of those for whom the legislation was framed have changed. We all know that when the first national housing bill was introduced it did not cover all the conditions we find in the legislation today. If the desire of those eligible for VLA smallholdings is to have retirement acreage or a smallholding on which to spend the last years of their lives, then so be it. Let us change the act to bring that about. But let us not cut if off
War Veterans
and give as an excuse the fact that the act was not designed as a retirement plan for veterans.
All this motion does is urge the government to bring in measures to remedy certain injustices in veterans pensions. There are 900,000 veterans still alive in Canada, of which about 78,000 receive war veterans allowances, 130,000 receive disability pensions and 30,000 widows and orphans get pensions. There are about 5,000 veterans in DVA hospitals, and about 60,000 benefiting from the Veterans Land Act program.
We urge the government to act on the joint study report passed unanimously by the standing committee, and to allow those receiving veterans benefits to live in dignity and be removed forever from the need to beg for increased allowances. We urge this government to act humanely and with compassion, and to introduce in the House the necessary legislation to enact the recommendations of the joint study group in respect of the basic rate of pensions.

speakeroldname: Mr. Charles Turner (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO IMPROVE PENSIONS AND REMOVE INJUSTICES TO WAR VETERANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make some comments about the Veterans Land Act and in so doing I think it appropriate to commence by referring to the title of the act and several pertinent sections of the preamble, the Veterans Land Act is entitled "An act to assist war veterans to settle upon the land". The preamble reads in part as follows:
Whereas many men now serving in the active forces of Canada have recorded their desire to settle on land or engage in farming when hostilities cease, and it is desirable that suitably qualified veterans be encouraged to seek rehabilitation in the agricultural industry;
And whereas part-time farming coupled with other employment is an increasingly important aspect of rural and semi-rural life in Canada,
And whereas it is in the public interest as a measure of rehabilitation to assist in acquiring the ownership of farm homes by qualified veterans .. .
And whereas the great majority of prospective veteran settlers have limited financial assets and the lack of such assets has proved to be the main obstacle to the fulfillment of settlement contracts and to the acquirement of farm home ownership;
And whereas it is the purpose of the Dominion Government to provide a measure of financial assistance to veterans on their performance of prescribed settlement conditions in order to promote their engaging in agricultural pursuits either as a full-time occupation or as a part-time occupation coupled with some other employment;-
I believe both the title of the act and those parts of the preamble to which I have referred make crystal clear what the intent, nature and purposes were conceived and understood to be when parliament, on behalf of a grateful country, enacted this rehabilitation measure more than a quarter of a century ago. It was not, of course, the only rehabilitation measure enacted. It was recognized that many veterans would not be interested or find it practical to settle on the land either as full or part-time farmers.
For such veterans, alternative benefits to those of the Veterans Land Act were provided. Here I refer to the university training allowances of the Veterans Rehabilitation Act and to re-establishment credits provided under the War Service Grants Act. Each veteran had the option
3936


War Veterans
of deciding which of these alternative benefits best suited his particular rehabilitation needs or desires.
With the benefit of hindsight, one might contend that an additional rehabilitation measure should have been enacted in 1946 to offer veterans special financial and other arrangements with respect to urban housing. In fact, because such provisions were not enacted I believe there has been intermittent pressure over the years to try to make the part-time farming provisions of the Veterans Land Act into housing legislation, a field of course that is and has been covered by the National Housing Act.
As I indicated at the beginning of my remarks, the purpose of the Veterans Land Act clearly was to encourage and assist veterans at the end of hostilities and on their return to civilian life to settle on the land as full or part-time farmers. I believe this purpose essentially has been achieved and with a degree of success beyond all expectations. Dealing solely with the category of full-time farming settlement, I understand almost 32,000 veterans have been established on either commercial or family farm units. Public funds advanced to these veterans, including the ten-year conditional grant benefit of up to $2,320, exceed $347 million. Well over 50 per cent of this number have already repaid their contracts and acquired title to their properties.
It would be unreasonable to expect, of course, that every veteran would succeed. When you consider, however, that less than 200 of these 32,000-just over one half of one per cent-have had their contracts with the director rescinded after consideration by and with the consent of provincial advisory boards, I think it is self-evident that the legislation was well conceived, has been well administered and has achieved the rehabilitation purpose envisaged.
I observed earlier that the Veterans Land Act was enacted more than a quarter of a century ago. Today the average age of veterans of World War II is approaching 56 or 57. This is not the time of life to undertake settlement on the land as a full-time farmer, a fact which is borne out both by the limited number of new farm establishments which are being made under the act and by the number of veterans who are repaying the director and acquiring title. In the calendar year 1972, less than 100 veterans were settled on farms, compared with 11,398 in the fiscal year 1946-47, and close to 700 terminated their contracts.
Undoubtedly, having regard to the basic purpose of the Veterans Land Act and the extended period which had already elapsed since the end of World War II, in 1965 parliament approved terminal dates for loan applications with the object of phasing out VLA lending operations in an orderly manner. Taking all circumstances into consideration, I find that I share the opinion expressed by the minister in his statement to the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs on March 6 last, when he said it appeared that the deadlines approved by parliament in 1965 were reasonable then and remain so.
Mr. Speaker, I have a few further comments to make about the Veterans Land Act and, in particular, about the provisions of the act which were designed to assist veterans of World War II, and later those of the Korean special force, to pick up the threads of civilian life following wartime active service by engaging in farming on a parttime basis coupled with off-farm employment. It is my

understanding that the concept behind the part-time farming or smallholding provisions of the act evolved in part from the economic and employment difficulties of the thirties when many Canadian families found it possible to overcome, or substantially abate those difficulties by supplementing their meagre or irregular income by what they could produce from the land. Even without the environmental benefits available in rural or semi-rural locations, which are today being recognized by an increasing number of citizens, I believe the concept was sound and reflective of the sense of independence and pride still inherent in the majority of the Canadian people.
Undoubtedly, because economic and employment circumstances for the most part in the 28 years which have elapsed since World War II have not demanded the same degree of agricultural utilization of land by those engaged principally in off-farm employment, there has been a growing tendency to look upon the smallholding provisions of the act primarily as a medium to obtain housing accommodation, in urban areas if at all possible, on favourable financial terms.
Urban housing involves, of course, a field of legislation for which the provisions of the National Housing Act have been particularly designed and are fully applicable. Hence, any further departure from the agriculture use concept of the smallholding sections of the Veterans Land Act would bring them into conflict with and duplicate the provisions of the National Housing Act. The inadvisability of permitting this to happen was, in fact, recognized almost 20 years ago. In 1954, following favourable consideration by government of a proposal made by the Royal Canadian Legion, part II of the Veterans Land Act was enacted to provide financial and other assistance to a veteran who was not interested in, or was unable to settle under, the smallholding provisions of the act but who wished to build his own house on a city size lot. More than 4,300 veterans have obtained building loans under part II.
Since the inception of VLA operations 30 years ago, approximately 90,000 veterans have obtained financial assistance under the small-holding provisions of the act, totalling over $826 million. New house construction was involved in more than one-third of these establishments, including 2,673 homes which were built by the director in 1945-46 to help overcome the housing shortage being encountered by veterans on their return from overseas. As with veterans settled as full-time farmers, those established as small-holders have been equally successful in fulfilling the obligations of their agreements of sale with the director. Almost 30,000 have repaid their loans and acquired title to their properties, and some 6,000 have arranged sales to other veterans. Only 150 contracts have had to be rescinded after consideration by and with the consent of provincial advisory boards.
As I stated at the beginning of my remarks, the parttime farming provisions of the Veterans Land Act were designed to assist in the rehabilitation of veterans following their wartime active service. Some 28 years have elasped since the end of World War II, and almost 20 in the case of the Korean conflict. It is difficult, therefore, to conceive a continuing need for the act as a post-war rehabilitation measure. In fact, of the representations I have received recently for an extension of the new estab-


lishment loan deadline of March 31, 1974, almost invariably the desire has been indicated of wanting to use the provisions of the act following retirement from post-war occupations or careers.
The benefits of the Veterans Land Act were alternative to university training and re-establishment credit. The university training program was concluded some 20 years ago. The final date for the use of re-establishment credits was October 31, 1968, which corresponded to the deadline for obtaining a VLA certificate of qualification. We are now approaching the terminal date for new settlement loan applications approved by parliament in 1965, and by next March more than 140,000 veterans will have obtained assistance, under the various sections of the act, of more than $1.1 billion. The Veterans Land Act has been an outstanding success.
In closing, I say to the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Beattie) that one of the largest land developers in the city of London is the national president of the Progressive Conservative party. At present he is working on a housing project almost at the back door of Westminster hospital. The hon. member can rest assured that so far as I am concerned he will never get his hands on this beautiful piece of property. I believe this property would make a beautiful city park for the benefit of all Canadians and veterans.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO IMPROVE PENSIONS AND REMOVE INJUSTICES TO WAR VETERANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will take note of the time limit and confine my remarks to ten minutes. I am interested in speaking on the motion in order to try to do something about the long delay of the government in introducing legislation the effect of which would be to implement the report of the joint study group on the basic rate of disability pension for veterans.
In the report of the joint study group there is a recommendation for not only a monetary increase for veterans but the introduction of a new and important principle. Veterans pensions are to be based on the standard of living; they will no longer be based on the cost of living. There is a very important difference here, because the rate of increase in the standard of living is twice that of the increase in the cost of living. If the cost of living goes up by 3 per cent, it follows that the standard of living goes up by 6 per cent. Therefore, this recommendation will be of definite benefit to our veterans in receipt of disability pensions.
War Veterans
I should like to repeat something that has been mentioned before, because I do not think it can be repeated too often and also to convince the government of our unanimity on the principle of an increase in basic pensions. In addition, I wish to give support to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) in his battle with his cabinet colleagues to bring this legislation forward. Let me point out again that every member of the parliamentary standing committee agreed within an hour to send this report back to the House and recommend that it be implemented. Certainly all veterans' organizations agreed, and the Minister of Veterans Affairs himself is in total agreement with it. Finally, it was the work of a group composed of representatives of veterans' organizations, members of the Pension Commission and members of our Department of Veterans Affairs.
What is the reason for the delay, then? It must lie in the cabinet itself. It has refused to accept the report of the committee to which I have referred and it has refused to accept the report of the Minister of Veterans Affairs. Surely among all members of the House he, better than anybody else, understands veterans because he is a veteran and he was seriously wounded in the defence of his country. He is a double amputee. Here is a man who above all men should be listened to when he makes a recommendation to the cabinet for some action.
It is difficult to understand why the minister's colleagues are so callous in their attitude toward those men and women who dropped their civilian status, left their work on farms, in fishing, in forestry, in the factory and in the office to take part in the war. These are the men and women who gave their lives so that freedom and democracy should not perish on this earth. Why, then, does it .take so long for a group of men to make up their minds to move on this vital issue?
Let us not quibble over a few paltry thousand, maybe million dollars. I think it is apparent to everybody, as I said before, that it is not the minister who is giving us trouble but, rather, the Treasury Board. Perhaps we could pin it right back on the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) himself, because I think he feels that if he takes this action it will be precedent-setting and other pensioners will then raise a hue and cry to have their pensions based on the standard of living. Surely the group of people with whom we are dealing is a very special group. Every member of the House and every Canadian knows what we owe these people. This benefit is only the just dues of a group of people who have earned it.
We hope very sincerely that the effect of this debate will strengthen the hand of the Minister of Veterans Affairs and will result in immediate action. I wonder sometimes if he should not carry some of his old hand-grenades into the cabinet meeting, pull the pin and say to his colleagues, "Look here, boys; it is time we settled this matter and brought the legislation forward". We hope that the debate today will have the effect of a hand-grenade under the seats of the people who are so tardy in taking this action.
I want to turn my attention for a brief minute or two to the Veterans Land Act which has been mentioned today. By and large, everybody agrees that it has been fairly administered except on one point. It seems to me that it is totally unrealistic, in today's situation with regard to


War Veterans
housing, that it should be required of a veteran that he own one-tenth of an acre before being eligible under the act for a grant to build a house. To purchase a lot of this size would require an astronomical sum of money. Nobody can afford to buy land of the size required in a residential area. Also, land suitable for the building of a house is too scarce; it is just not available. In addition, the municipal building by-laws would not permit the sale of this size of lot in a subdivision where a veteran would wish to build a house.
The veteran's increasing age makes it necessary that he locate his house, not out in the country somewhere where one could perhaps purchase a tenth of an acre on a farm but in a city, town or village where facilities, goods and services which he requires in his declining years are readily available. We raised this matter at one time in the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs when the director in charge of the Veterans Land Act was present. He said it would not be fair to change the rules in the middle of the game. I submit that we are in a totally different ball game today from the time this act was first set up and these conditions laid down. I think it would be difficult for anyone to remember the conditions which existed at the time this legislation was brought into effect.
In conclusion, I have a final few words with regard to the cut-off date of March 31, 1974, when the veteran should take up his option to take advantage of the provisions of the Veterans Land Act and build his own house. If the government is adamant in sticking to this deadline, which it says it is, then I think this date should be given the widest possible publicity as it approaches, let no veteran say that he did not know it was coming. We can make it known through the veterans' magazines and through letters to veterans, if we know their address; and I know this is a problem because the department does not know the current addresses of many veterans.
Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, I have used more than my allotted time. I know others want to speak on this motion, but I think we cannot stress too strongly the need for cabinet action to bring forth legislation to give effect to this very important principle of standard of living escalation for veterans disability pensions.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO IMPROVE PENSIONS AND REMOVE INJUSTICES TO WAR VETERANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it bodes well for the veterans of this country that so many hon. members wish to participate in this all-important debate that we must limit ourselves to ten minutes in order to allow all hon. members to have their say. The veterans should be cheered by this show of interest demonstrated by members on both sides of the House.
With all the splendid improvements in veterans legislation over the past few years one might expect to see a certain amount of complacency set in with respect to veterans affairs. But not so, Mr. Speaker. I suggest that this is not the case, due in large measure to the man who now holds the portfolio of Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald), who has seen to it that that portfolio will remain a lively one, introducing legislation with beneficial changes for our veterans. Not to be forgotten is the fact that all the government's legislation introduced for the benefit of veterans is available for their use.
[Mr. Knowles (Norfolk-Haldimand).l
It seems to me that in a debate on a motion such as this it would be very easy for a member of the government or a supporter of the government to say that we have done so much and to pat ourselves on the back. But I do not think this should be the role of a government member. I also think that the Minister of Veterans Affairs put his case very well today and it does not need any supplementary argument from me.
In the previous parliament I had the honour of serving as a member, as vice-chairman and as chairman of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs. This has been one of the highlights of my short parliamentary career thus far, and it may be the reason why I am still receiving letters from veterans all across Canada. One of the things disturbing them is the long delay in rulings upon applications for disability pensions. Today I was very pleased to hear of the changes that have been made to reduce these delays, one of them being a 14 per cent increase in the size of the staff. This should help cut down the delays and should cut into the backlog of cases that must be heard. I was also interested to hear the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Guay) indicate that the backlog of cases does not comprise simple cases, that most cases need a lot of research and a lot of work. Fortunately, we now have the personnel to do that sort of job.
I for one, Mr. Speaker, welcome the idea of the department moving out of the hospital field and the action already taken in that regard. As veterans get older there will be less tendency for physicians to take up work in veterans hospitals, because there they will be treating similar ailments; they will be dealing only with the geriatric type of disease. Because our veterans are entitled to the best care we should get them into the best hospitals. But, Mr. Speaker, that is going only part of the way. There is no suggestion of reducing the amount of money by having them cared for in other hospitals, and I suggest that the department has an obligation to follow up these transfers, to keep an eye on veterans and to see if they are properly treated and given the particular attention they deserve. I would also like to see the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs perform a grand jury role and visit hospitals on an annual basis, talking to the veterans in them in order to make sure that they are getting the care and the attention they have earned.
I welcome the action taken by the minister so far as European prisoners of war are concerned. I have had great interest in the POW situation over the past five years. I know that former ministers made provision for a study of the files of veterans who had been prisoners of war to see if there was a common ailment running through them. Unfortunately, the files do not show many things that are bothering veterans. Many people have had nervous breakdowns and these are not shown in the records. That is why I welcome the study being conducted now by Dr. Hermann. He, too, is studying the files and meeting with veterans groups. I note that he has sent out a questionnaire. In my local newspaper I inserted a plea that veterans not be apathetic about that questionnaire. I pleaded with them to fill out the forms so that Dr. Hermann will be in a position to make a comprehensive report for the consideration of the department.


One other matter I would like to deal with is the pension paid to widows. At present there is a 48 per cent cut-off. If a veteran had 48 per cent disability, then his widow on his death would draw the widow's pension; but if he had disability beneath that level, she could not draw the pension. I believe consideration should be given to paying the widow a proportionate share of the pension. If her husband had 30 per cent disability, why not pay her 30/48"" of the full pension.

I have been fighting for this for five years. My mother fell into that category, so I know something about it. With respect to the Veterans Land Act, having listened to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Turner), I think his point is well taken so far as the Veterans Land Act is concerned. But I agree with the hon. member for Norfolk-Haldimand (Mr. Knowles) that we should be looking into the question of a new act. We have been receiving requests from veterans about the kind of assistance available under the act and I believe the department should circulate a questionnaire to find out how many veterans would be interested in taking advantage of a new Veterans Land Act. In that way we could discover positive recommendations for legislation.
I also think the time has arrived for passage of the basic rate legislation. This point has been made by others more eloquent than I am. I know that the minister is doing all he can to bring the matter to a head, and I do not think it is being delayed at the cabinet level. subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO IMPROVE PENSIONS AND REMOVE INJUSTICES TO WAR VETERANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the interests of saving time and allowing others to contribute to this debate, and to provide the minister with that additional strength which we all want him to have to take this matter to cabinet, I will not use a number of introductory remarks that I had ready. There are two areas of interest to which I will be turning my attention, but before doing so I want to remind all of us about something we owe our veterans.
There are many things we owe the veterans of this country, but let none of us forget that a great deal of the prestige enjoyed by Canada in world affairs today is due to the commitment of thousands of Canadians in uniform in the various theatres of war in which Canada shared the burden of horror and the glory of victory. Our stance at the United Nations, in NATO and on the world scene at large is in no small measure due to the selfless service our veterans gave to their fellow countrymen and to mankind. This is the background against which we should be considering these matters today.
There are in my riding many classes of veterans. There are some with longstanding claims to benefits of one kind or another. None wants to be a mendicant, yet unfortunately many of these veterans are obliged to adopt tactics that no self-respecting citizens, especially our veterans, should be forced to take. Our veterans should not be put in that position. They are proud men and they have reason to be proud.
War Veterans
My remarks this afternoon are confined to two particular sections-veterans hospitals and pensions to servicemen who retired early because of the age-rank formula at a time when salaries were well below the national average.
In respect of the veterans hospitals and the facilities offered to veterans there, I speak particularly about the veterans hospital in Victoria which serves many of my constituents. Reports are circulating in the area and it came to my ears earlier this week that negotiations between the federal government and the province of British Columbia relating to takeover of that hospital have been concluded or are nearing conclusion. I hope these reports are incorrect, because I would remind the minister that about three weeks ago he wrote a letter to me indicating that nothing that could be described as negotiations were in sight at that time, although conversations on the matter had been under way for some time. It would cause me considerable discomfort and worry to learn that he can say one thing to me in writing and yet sanction the continuance of negotiations to take over that hospital.
Whether we are at the conversation or the negotiation stage, I am wondering what action the minister is taking to reassure those who have an undeniable claim on the services of that hospital that they will continue to enjoy their earned rights. It is indeed my view that more should be done to provide this reassurance. Many of my constituents are worried and asked me for reassurance, and I give it on the strength of the letters I receive from the minister. However, not being in the government I cannot give them that assurance with the same effect as the minister can. i therefore urge that the minister speak specifically to this matter and reassure these people. It is all the more necessary, I submit, in view of correspondence that I have in my office and the rumours that none the less continue to circulate. I merely bring this to the attention of the minister so that the matter can be corrected.
My other concern, and the concern of a very large number of my constituents and of many ex-servicemen across the country, is with the pensions they receive because they retired in that period of our development, in the late forties, fifties and sixties, when their salaries, the base on which the pensions are calculated, were abnormally depressed below the wage and salary levels in effect across Canada. Meanwhile, those who remained in the service saw their salaries increase, so that when their time comes to retire they will have a base that will provide what might be called a livable pension, at least much more livable than those whose base in some instances was as low as $4,000 and few higher than $12,000, as compared with the $10,000, $12,000 and $25,000-range bases that exist today.
An escalation formula seems to be necessary, therefore, and it has been adopted in certain limited circumstances. Something much more energetic must be done in this area to take into account two significant developments: first, the salary increases that have occurred since these servicemen had to retire and, second, the inflationary forces that are attacking veterans pensions and pensions for all Canadians-all pensions, from whatever war. Something must be done to prevent these pensions withering away under the searing wind of inflation.


War Veterans
I thank you, Mr. Speaker, and I hope others will cover those aspects of this question which I should have liked to deal with. I am sure this debate will provide the minister with the ammunition he needs to convince cabinet that much more must be done, and done urgently.

Mr. Speaker, I, too, would like to congratulate the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall) for the presentation of his motion this afternoon. We have had already some discussion of veterans affairs during this session of parliament, but I think that now we can isolate, in the debate on this resolution, those points which are still outstanding.
We have some converts, or spokesmen on the government side for these particular points. I must say, however, that I was somewhat disappointed in the minister's reply. I know that nothing has been mentioned about the European theatre of war prisoners, but that the matter is in hand and I am glad to see that progress has been made. I am anxiously awaiting progress reports. I have yet to meet a prisoner of war who has been contacted, and I am wondering just how the choice is made.

speechtext: Were you?

speechtext:
No, but I am a living symbol of all the bad things that came out of it. Regardless of that, I am just wondering how extensive the sampling will be. I have heard some rather odd rumours about the surveys that are being made. Some of the questions may be considered to be rather prying regarding the present level of income, the present value of property occupied, etc. I do not want to compare them with veterans who were not prisoners of war and civilians to see what the position is, but there may be an argument for that. However, I should like to see the package before I agree to it.
I am glad that the hon. member for Sarnia-Lambton (Mr. Cullen), the former chairman of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs, has voiced support for the changes to benefit the widow of a veteran pensioner whose entitlement was less than 48 per cent. We urged this as far back as 1963. The cost of giving a portion of a deceased veteran's pension to his widow is minimal.
Starting four or five years ago one could see the attitude of cabinet toward veterans affairs. They did come through with some things, but reluctantly, and that was only after hard pressure. Perhaps this is just because of the composition of cabinet, because the age group is different. I hope the younger members of this House are not infected with the idea that I have heard some young people express today-"They have had their war and it is a matter of history. We do not need the parades and ceremonies; let's forget about it. They have written about it in books and it is all there." This is the rather callous, unheeding attitude of those who fail to recognize that if it had not been for the sacrifices of those men and women, the young persons of today would not have the opportunity of moving about and enjoying life as they do.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO IMPROVE PENSIONS AND REMOVE INJUSTICES TO WAR VETERANS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO IMPROVE PENSIONS AND REMOVE INJUSTICES TO WAR VETERANS
speechtext:
The same thing applies in many, many countries. So I say a great debt is

owed to a person who is totally disabled today. One has merely to go through the veterans hospitals to see what the results have been.
One matter on which I must criticize the minister is in regard to the veteran who is residing overseas and who has not come back to qualify under the 12-month residence clause. The minister has said that matter is under review. I would say this question has come under active pressure, certainly from me, for six years and I am sick to the teeth of hearing the same blessed reasons. These are administrative matters. Frankly, considering the limited number of people in the United Kingdom who might be subject to this benefit-there are about 700-the difficulty, with a little bit of good will and the elimination of some of the tunnel vision that seems to exist at certain levels of the department, could be overcome. I could show the minister letters and replies, not from the previous minister but from the minister before that who was not even interested in this subject.
Let me make my last point. I must berate the hon. member for London East (Mr. Turner), the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour, for giving this House the same sort of answer with regard to the Veterans Land Act that has been contained in correspondence from 1971 on. Young veterans who have been in the forces and are now retiring have been kept in the forces because they were wired in, so to speak, under a pension scheme. The minister must know the effect of that wiring in. After so many years in the service, the serviceman pretty well has to stay in until his time has expired; otherwise he would lose too much under the servicemen's pension provisions. That veteran is now coming out. His contributions and sacrifices were as great as those of any veteran who got out of the service at the end of the war and availed himself of the veterans charter. He was in a position to avail himself of it; he took a claim check on it. The only trouble is that the government and the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) are saying, "That claim check has now been discounted; it is worth only one-tenth of what it was worth." Entitlement is proportionate to relevant service.
Of course, we are not going to set up an agricultural rehabilitation program, any more than we would set up the homestead program that we set up after World War I. After World War II we did not ask the men to homestead as we had done after World War I. We are dealing with another generation now, and housing is the question that these people must face. The provisions of the Veterans Land Act are adequate; but, today just walk around any city and see how much these men would have to pay.
The department insists on half an acre, with some modifications. Mr. Speaker, the purpose of the Veterans Land Act is no longer that of turning veterans into farmers or part-time farmers. We are asking veterans to find an equity of $10,000, $15,000 or $18,000 simply because the government refuses to increase the ceiling on advances that can be made under the Veterans Land Act. Veterans are told, and I have correspondence to this effect, that they can go to CMHC.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO IMPROVE PENSIONS AND REMOVE INJUSTICES TO WAR VETERANS
speechtext: Shame.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO IMPROVE PENSIONS AND REMOVE INJUSTICES TO WAR VETERANS
speechtext:
They are told to take their chances there. So in cases of that kind, what is the worth of the veterans charter? Our veterans are told it is not worth the paper it is written on. Borrowing ceilings are limited. These loans are not going to cost the government or the taxpayer more money, because mortgages are taken out. These moneys that are advanced to the veteran are repayable. The terms may be a little easier than those he would get from CMHC or a conventional mortgage company, but that was the very purpose of the scheme at the beginning. So why take the advantage away from him in this case?
I urge these considerations on the minister. I have correspondence on these subjects, some acknowledged, some not acknowledged. I have letters that repeat, frankly, the same out of date arguments as were put forward by the hon. member for London East in justification of the present attitude regarding the Veterans Land Act. In so many words they say, "The veterans program was determined by this government to be a running down program." I should like to see any minister of veterans affairs walk into a Canadian Legion hall tonight and say that the veterans program is a running down program. I wonder how long he would last.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO IMPROVE PENSIONS AND REMOVE INJUSTICES TO WAR VETERANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, recognizing that we are running short of time, I shall be brief. I welcome this opportunity to take part, as a new member, in my first debate on veterans affairs. I say this with considerable, feeling as my father was a veteran of the First World War and as, in a modest way, I served with the armed forces of my country some years ago
I represent a riding in which there are a great many veterans and veterans' dependents, many of whom were in my constituency before I was elected. I have heard from them about some things which, under the present law, did not seem in their view to be right and I want to bring these to the attention of the minister and the House. In particular I wish to mention a matter that was brought to my attention by a lady of my riding, Mrs. Rodgers, whose husband, Archibald Graham Rodgers, was a soldier in the Canadian army and died recently. He was a veteran of the Second World War and served with the Royal Canadian Artillery, being wounded in action and mentioned in dispatches. As a result, he was awarded a pension of less than 48 per cent. As a consequence of his death, the pension has now lapsed and his widow and children are not able to benefit from it. His widow, Mrs. Rodgers, has said to me that this should be brought to the attention of hon. members of this House, and I agree with her.
It seems to me that there is an inconsistency in a pension system which is geared to help the veteran and his family but which, just when the family has the greatest need for money, takes it away. The second thing Mrs. Rodgers brought to my attention was that the entitlement to the option under the Veterans Land Act, an option
War Veterans
which expires in March, 1974, expires if the veteran dies before that time. Again, I think she is right in saying that this does not make sense, inasmuch as the benefit which this country properly gave to its veterans will not go to the loved ones, to the family of the veteran, in case of death.
It is not always that members mention individual cases in the House. In the case of this widow and her now deceased veteran husband I thought it proper that the House hear that the sacrifices he made and the principles for which he fought have been mentioned by the widow to her Member of Parliament. Therefore I have had the privilege of bringing this matter to the attention of the House and am grateful for the consideration and attention I have received.
May I mention something else, Mr. Speaker. Reports from British Columbia indicate that the recent raises in veterans pensions have not been reflected in any increase in that province. I am sure the minister is aware of this and I hope he will give the matter consideration. Lastly, let me repeat a verse that was contained in a book about soldiering and the armed forces that someone gave me many years ago. The verse is part of an old sonnet which has come down, from hundreds of years ago. It goes like this:
God and the soldier we alike adore,
In times of danger, not before.
The danger gone, all things requited,
God is forgotten, the soldier slighted.
I think there is great truth in that old verse. However, I know that all members are united in their determination not to allow this to happen to our soldiers. Posterity will not say that that is an attitude of which we are guilty.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO IMPROVE PENSIONS AND REMOVE INJUSTICES TO WAR VETERANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to join with virtually all members who have spoken in this debate this afternoon to urge the government to take action now to increase the veterans war disability pension. As a former member of the Royal Canadian Air Force and now a member of the Legion in my constituency, I have had of course direct contact with men and women who are concerned about the veterans' increase.
The Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) has since assuming this portfolio done a great job for the veterans of Canada. I join the debate simply to ask him to extend the good work he has done to include this one category that so far has been excluded from significant improvement. On behalf of the government, the minister has promised an increase in the war disability pension but it has not yet been brought forward. We have not yet received a clear indication of the time when that change will be made. I suspect the minister is having a little trouble with the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury), and perhaps with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), in getting the needed financial resources to implement what I know he desires.
If the efforts of members of all parties can lead to a change in the attitude of the government, surely the debate this afternoon-which is a rare expression of virtu-


War Veterans
al unanimity on an issue-should provide additional support for the Minister in cabinet. I do not want to take the time of the House to repeat the points made by many others. This is an important area of concern. Major improvement is needed. The minister has indicated he wants to take action. The time for action is now.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO IMPROVE PENSIONS AND REMOVE INJUSTICES TO WAR VETERANS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO IMPROVE PENSIONS AND REMOVE INJUSTICES TO WAR VETERANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members who have spoken in this debate have indicated their strongest support for immediate action to bring into line the disability pension. Customarily, when there has been reform of the veterans charter the reform has not proceeded on a piecemeal basis but right across the board.
One of the reasons this great concern has been expressed in this debate is that we have proceeded to increase the war veterans allowance and there has been delay in a similar increase in the disability pension. I hope that as a result of this resolution now before the House-and indeed this is the main purpose of it-the minister's hand will be strengthened and he will be able to convince the government that this matter requires the utmost priority.
The term "utmost priority" is quite frequently used with regard to governmental expenditures. One of the criticisms of the present administration is that it has its priorities upside down; it is dealing with shadow issues rather than substance issues. The group of veterans in this country who were faced with the ultimate priority, the survival of the thin fabric of democracy, should have the first consideration.
I want to make one other observation in this brief presentation, that is, to point out that the issues have been clearly laid down by veterans' organizations in this country. No one has to be uncertain as to where the priorities lie. I pay tribute to them. I hope their petitions, pleas, presentations and briefs will be reinforced by what has taken place here today.
There is one particular veterans' group I wish to mention at this time. That is the Polish Combatants Association which is meeting in Ottawa this weekend. It is the fifteenth conference of that association. They are honouring one of the outstanding veterans of World War II, General S. Kopanski. A lunch was sponsored today by the Minister of State responsible for multiculturalism (Mr. Haidasz) which was attended by General Kopanski. General Kopanski and his Polish comrades were the first to meet the onslaught of the totalitarian system. He is known as the hero of Tobruk. Had the supermen not been stopped at Tobruk in 1941, the history of civilization would have been changed. The Polish soldiers under the leadership of General Kopanski played a large role in that victory.
I mention these gentlemen because in their comments at the luncheon today they expressed gratitude to a former minister of veterans affairs from the Maritimes, the late Colonel Alf Brooks who during his term of office in this important portfolio undertook a major review of the veterans charter. It was as a result of that review that the members of the Polish Association Combatants, the SPK, now resident in Canada were given full benefits under the Canadian veterans charter. Colonel Brooks is typical of

the many members of this House who have held the veterans affairs portfolio. I think the present incumbent would give the same emphasis and consideration that was given by the hon. gentleman to whom I have referred. Today is the twenty-ninth anniversary of the victory at Monte Cassino. In view of the convention taking place in Ottawa this weekend, it is interesting to note that the Canadian and Polish soldiers fought side by side in order to achieve that crucial victory.
There is one main consideration. Equalization of the pension rates at this time should have been considered simultaneously with the increase in the war veterans allowance. There is one other point I would like to raise. The benefit of the doubt clause for these veterans, who in many cases made the supreme sacrifice and engaged in the ultimate priority, is still not being adequately applied to veterans in their pension applications. I remind the minister, too, that the current backlog of pension applications is causing unnecessary hardship to these men to whom we owe so much.
All members of this House have indicated that they will give immediate consideration to the necessary legislation. I trust that as a result of this debate the minister will be able to get action through the cabinet.
