Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity given me to comment on the National Veterans Association and specifically on their representations.
The War Veterans Act has been amended so often that veterans indeed like many other citizens, enjoy greater advantages, but there are still major inequities to be corrected. We request amendment of the act in order that those who have been left out may benefit more by it. In fact, in such associations, certains classes or individuals are always neglected.
We are pleased about the pension increase. We are aware that the budget provided for pension increases for veterans as well as for certain other groups. The budget provided for a number of increases, such as for old age security and disability pensions.
The claims of national veterans organizations are based on a calculation of adjusted incomes, and not just on a means test. These adjustments, Mr. Speaker, are a considerable help to those whose income is limited at a time when the cost of living is rising.
Mr. Speaker, we are in favour of the pension increase, but with certain reservations. We are aware that we will not solve the basic problems by continually raising pensions. We must see to the foundation of our economy. The more we raise pensions, the more we raise the cost of services.
We are aware, Mr. Speaker, that the correct solution does not involve throwing the economy off balance. The economy needs basic rebalancing, and I wish to point this out to my fellow members because we are elected to rectify the deficiencies that exist in our society. By raising pensions of all kinds we get into a visious circle. It puts up


the cost of living, and the more that increases, the more the economy is thrown off balance.
Mr. Speaker, if we want to stabilize our economy once again, we will have to use means other than those we have used until now. We will have to modify our structures because a succession of increases will lead inevitably to economic suicide.
Mr. Speaker, the more we raise pensions, the closer we get to an increasingly centralizing state and the use of progressively less revealing and less honest means for the citizens, because as they get higher pensions they lose part of their freedom. And so, Mr. Speaker, we are fighting to protect our freedom.
We also know, Mr. Speaker, and I should like to point it out before closing, that-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: CONSIDERATION OF OBJECTIONS TO REPORT OF NEWFOUNDLAND COMMISSION
speechtext:
On April 18, 1973, notice of objection in the form of a motion was filed with Mr. Speaker in the following terms:
That, pursuant to section 20 of the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act, (Chapter E-2, R.S.C. 1970), consideration be given by this House to the matter of an objection to the provisions of the report of the Electoral Boundaries Commission for the province of Newfoundland, laid before this House by Mr. Speaker on Thursday, April 5, 1973, on the grounds set forth hereafter:
1.	Throughout Newfoundland the commission failed to give special emphasis to geographical considerations, the sparsity, density and relative rate of growth of the population, and ignored or overlooked the special problems of communication and transportation when they divided the said province into six new electoral districts.
2.	The commission failed to give special consideration and special appreciation to accessibility of one region to another region in many of the rural electoral districts when determining the boundaries of the same.
3.	The commission failed to pay proper attention to the physical, social or economic cohesion of many of the new electoral districts created and appeared to ignore and did ignore the question of unity or community of interests thereby rendering
Electoral Boundaries
adequate representation of the people in Parliament a virtually impossible task.
4.	The commission failed to take into consideration that the boundaries of the majority of electoral districts of Newfoundland as they existed prior to redistribution were in accordance with the spirit of the terms of union between Newfoundland and Canada.
5.	The inconvenience to any Member of Parliament attempting to maintain contact with constituents spread over some electoral districts would be considerable. The expense of travel in attempting to maintain such contact might well be considered exorbitant.
6.	And such other objections that the undersigned Members may consider applicable in order to carry out the spirit and terms and conditions of the act in question.

speakeroldname: Mr. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subsubtopic: CONSIDERATION OF OBJECTIONS TO REPORT OF NEWFOUNDLAND COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall be very brief. In accordance with the provisions of the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act we have to commence this debate today. The objections to the report of the Electoral Boundaries Commission are set out in the letter which was filed with Your Honour on April 13 and read into the record a few moments ago by Your Honour.
We object to the report of the commission because it fails to take into account all the arguments which we have set out in the letter which will appear in today's record. More particularly, we base our objection on the fact that the province of Newfoundland under the report now before the House will lose a seat and will be placed in the anomalous position of having fewer seats in parliament today than was the case 23 years ago when Newfoundland became a province of Canada and had a population one-third less than it has today.
We should also be placed in the anomalous position of having four seats fewer than the province of New Brunswick, which has virtually the same population but which is protected by the provisions of the House of Commons Act by virtue of which that province has ten seats in the other place. We, of course, have six seats in the other place; consequently, we feel the province will be underrepresented if this report goes through.
I urge upon the government that it take every step possible to ensure that Newfoundland shall continue to receive adequate representation in this House. We feel that if the report now before the House is adopted, the province will not, and indeed cannot be adequately represented because of the fact that we shall lose a seat, and because the six seats which are to be set up under the report of the commission do not take into account community of interest and all the difficulties which would be encountered by those who would be called upon to represent the province within the proposed new boundaries. Their task would be made more difficult, if not impossible.

speakeroldname: Mr. William Rompkey (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subsubtopic: CONSIDERATION OF OBJECTIONS TO REPORT OF NEWFOUNDLAND COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my first objection really does not lie within the terms of reference of the commission because I do not think its terms of reference were to deal with the question of six seats as such. The first point I wish to make is that Newfoundland cannot be adequately represented by six seats. We are a big province. Labrador alone is over 112,000 square miles in extent. We need more seats. I urge the government to consider the arguments put forward and to increase the number of seats beyond six, possibly to seven or even eight.


Electoral Boundaries
What concerns me more every day is the question of representation, the quality of representation we can give as Members of Parliament if we have constituencies such as Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador or Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe. I am picking out the two which are largest in geographical area and which are among the most difficult to travel around. While I am quite prepared to serve one of those constituencies, and will do so to the very best of my ability-I am speaking about the people from Grand Falls to Nain-there is a limit to what any one person can do.
If we are to represent our constituencies properly, we need either a redistribution of boundaries or extra help as Members of Parliament, particularly today when large corporations and governments have such control over people's lives. Far be it from me as a new Member of Parliament to presume to tell other hon. members what the duties of an MP should be, but it seems to me that emphasis ought to be placed on the role of an MP as an ombudsman. It is all very well to get up and make speeches in the House of Commons, but I see an increasing need for a buffer between the individual and corporations or government departments whose activities increasingly affect his life and over which he has so little control.
From this point of view, I think our difficulties will be seriously increased by the boundaries which have been drawn. These boundaries do not take into account the changes that have taken place in Newfoundland since 1949. I do not want to be political about these changes; I simply want to say that the boundaries were drawn up when Newfoundland was a collection of bays. It is no longer a collection of bays; it is now a province with highways and access roads. We have improved transportation and communications; Newfoundland is not the same now as it was in 1949. The redistribution that has taken place does not recognize or take into account that fact, and the boundary lines bear no relation to changes that have gone on in the province.
Let me give an example. The line drawn down the northern peninsula of Newfoundland makes no sense whatever. I am sure my colleague for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall) would agree that the problems are the same on his side of the peninsula as they are on mine. It would seem to me that this type of matter was not recognized when these lines were drawn with respect to redistribution, so I think there are excellent arguments for redrawing the lines.
The final point I want to make is this, and I have made it before. I represent the unique area of Labrador. It has much more in common, really, with the Northwest Territories and the Yukon than it does with the island of Newfoundland, but it is legally a part of the province as determined by the 1927 boundary agreement and the decision of the British Privy Council. It has unique geographic, economic and cultural problems. These problems are difficult and require attention. They are just now coming to full flower. If we are to really make that part of the province an integral part, we must solve the transportation and communication problems in that area.

As I said before, I speak for the people of Newfoundland because I am sure they want to see Labrador become an integral part of the province. If we are to move in this direction we must do justice to these people. I would therefore recommend to the commission that when it redraws these boundaries it considers establishing a seat for the district of Labrador alone, for the reasons I have enunciated.
In conclusion, I must say I do not agree that we should cut down the number of seats to six. We need more representation, and I urge the government to increase the number. Secondly, I suggest the boundary lines bear no resemblance to actual reality in the province and require major readjustment.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the couple of minutes I have at my disposal I want to support the objections raised by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath). I appeared before the commission when it sat in the city of Corner Brook in my riding of Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe, and I was astounded when the chairman of the commission told me that when I had another 112,000 square miles added to my district I would still have the easiest district in Newfoundland to cover. I do not know what was wrong with that judge.
The legislation which authorizes redistribution works directly against the purposes for which hon. members are here in parliament. Everyone knows how vast the workload of Members of Parliament has become. People are looking to members for advice and assistance, and at the same time we have a duty to visit our ridings. This whole procedure, to my mind, is not smart and does not make sense. I support the objections and hope, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) indicated some time ago, that changes will be made to the British North America Act which will make representation by population or by geographic area more relevant to the age in which we live.

subsubtopic: CONSIDERATION OF OBJECTIONS TO REPORT OF NEWFOUNDLAND COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not expect to have so much time at my disposal because I honestly thought the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall) would continue for the next couple of minutes. I just want to second the motion, if you will, which has been proposed today and commend my three colleagues on the arguments that have been presented. Those arguments are fundamental. The people of Newfoundland are against the whole concept as it has been perpetrated in the last couple of years and has come to the forefront today. The people are very concerned.
I speak today not as a Member of Parliament concerned about political interests but, rather, on behalf of the people who have widespread concern about what is happening in the province. They feel there is something radically wrong when a decision is made in 1973 to reduce representation from seven seats to six seats, particularly in view of what has happened to our population. Newfoundland has over 200,000 more people today than it had in 1949.
Those who recommended these redistribution changes must have had some principle in mind that is not well known, because their recommendations are against all


common sense and good reason. We were not allowed to present to the commission our arguments against this proposal. I, personally, filed my intention to present such arguments to that noteworthy judge-perhaps that is a bad choice of words-

subsubtopic: CONSIDERATION OF OBJECTIONS TO REPORT OF NEWFOUNDLAND COMMISSION
speechtext: "Noteworthy."

subsubtopic: CONSIDERATION OF OBJECTIONS TO REPORT OF NEWFOUNDLAND COMMISSION
speechtext:
Yes, perhaps I have said "noteworthy." My intention to present these objections to the proposed number of seats was overruled and I was not allowed to do so. That is one of the reasons we are making these objections today. There is no need to repeat all the objections, but I want to make one final point before we call it five o'clock, in the hope we can proceed later with the debate.
Something has been happening in Canada in the past half a century with which we as Members of Parliament must take issue today. We are using Newfoundland today as the basis for this particular debate, but this has been taking place across Canada in the last half century. I refer to the urban drift. Most great leaders in our country are unable to cope with the problems facing our urban society. We are now seeing the signs and signals of what could in a decade very well turn into a drift away from rural areas. People are placing a great deal more emphasis on material things and the quality of life than they did half a century ago.
It is incumbent upon legislators, whether on a national or provincial basis, to discourage the population movement to urban centres in Canada. Consequently, the government of this country has a responsibility to maintain the number of seats in rural parts of Canada rather than allow them to decrease, thereby diminishing the power and strength exerted by rural Canada. In view of these events now unfolding, I think we will find that the people in western Canada have a great deal in common with those of us who live in the eastern rural parts of this country. If the trend continues we will not have the same power in confederation which has been traditionally ours.
With regard to the United States, I read recently that the agricultural society in that country has been protected by the constitution and as a result the government cannot
Electoral Boundaries
ignore that sector as a political force. We are rapidly reaching the point that if we are not careful, or if we overlook the rural parts of Canada and allow a diminishing of political power in those areas, representation there will have no part in the decision-making in this country. This is what is of importance.
The hon. member for St. John's East referred to the confederation of states. We all know what effect this has on civilization. Many people in this country have great concern about the decision-making process. We now have only seven Members of Parliament. In the entire Atlantic provinces we have only 32 members at the present time, just a few more than the city of Toronto. Consequently politicians, being what they are, frequently favour areas with the largest political representation and make decisions on that basis. Very often this is not to the advantage of the country as a whole.
In conclusion, we think amendments must be made to rectify the situation. In this country today there are many points of dissension; not all of them are in Quebec or in the Atlantic provinces. Many of these dissensions are the result of lack of reasonableness on the part of our central government and its system and work to the disadvantage of various regions of the country.
Before calling it five o'clock, I should like, on behalf of my colleagues in the House of Commons, not just those from Newfoundland, to appeal to the government to do something to rectify these decisions.
